utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Can you hear me? For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis. To my left is our Case Manager, Sebastiaan van Hooydonk. To my right, Joanna Korner, Matthew Olmsted, Rafael La Cruz, and Alex Demirdjian. And on the back row, the two gentlemen are a couple of our interns, Edin Cengic and Nedim Muminovic is closest to the court reporter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, Michelle Butler, Miroslav Cuskic, Milena Dzudovic and Joyce Boekestijn, appearing for Zupljanin Defence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we begin, we've been alerted that the parties may wish to raise a housekeeping matter with reference to tomorrow's scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that was going to be me, but I've spoken to the Defence about the matter, which was the possibility of starting at 9.00 by going to Courtroom III. I had, of course, completely forgotten that Mr. Krgovic is in the case which is being heard before and so, unfortunately, it doesn't look as though we can do anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I asked Mr. Hannis very kindly if I may encroach for five minutes on his time just to deal with two matters relating to Zupljanin that I -- in my rush to try and finish, I meant to deal with yesterday. Your Honours will recall that I referred to a document which he had sent to the minister on the 20th of July. And can I ask that document P583 be put up. This is a document which is addressed, in fact, to the minister, or it's addressed to the MUP but headed underneath that for the minister although it is not on the part we've got up in the screen, and it begins by talking about the armed conflicts between the forces of the Serbian republic and the Muslim Croat and the first sentence reads: "We have informed you about the progress and the results of those conflicts on a regular basis." As I said, Mr. Hannis will be dealing with the matter of communications in a moment. It then goes on to deal with the various categories of people who have been imprisoned, and it talks about, as you will see on the screen, the -- Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honours. I'm going to ask -- I'm sorry. I'm afraid it's my fault. We've obviously got the wrong bits up. Could we put up the whole document instead. It makes it easier. Yes. Thank you. As you will see, dated the 20th of July, and there's the -- the sentence I've just referred to. And then it goes on to deal with the numbers of people arrested. And it talks about the three categories, and Your Honours will recall those categories are referred to in various documents that emanate from Prijedor and Sanski Most. And at the bottom of that paragraph the last independence: "The third category is made of adult men on which so far the service doesn't have any information of security interest for us, so they can be treated as hostages."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, who send this is letter?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to the bottom, Your Honours, will see the next page. It's sent by Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it then goes on to suggest various solutions. Perhaps if we just look at those solutions we can see on that page. The charges should be raised against persons for whom the service has documentary proof, persons, old persons, if any of them assume a decisive attitude. Now, Your Honours, what we say is this whole document is indicative of Zupljanin's attitude towards the prisoners, his knowledge as well. It doesn't say release them. It says: "Assume a decisive attitude to exchange military men of no security interest to us who can be treated as hostages." And, Your Honours, we say that whole document, exemplifies the attitude of Zupljanin towards these prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, your highlighting of this paragraph, this concluding phrase in this paragraph, apart from the -- anything that might have been -- any concepts that may have been lost in the translation, what comes over in the English, what, in your submission, was -- is that intended to convey?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The -- the -- the suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, we say instead of -- in particular, paragraph 2, instead of saying part of the Defence case against Mr. Zupljanin is that he didn't know about prisoners, and when he did know, he was prepared to deal with them in a proper manner and have them released. We say this document shows the very contrary. He's not doing anything of the sort. He's talking about hostages. He's talking about assume a decisive attitude. And all of this is being sent to the minister, his co-accused, Mico Stanisic. I hope that's clear, Your Honours. And, Your Honours, we say that one of the points that is made, if you look and we come back to that at the very end of what we say, is that -- that the Defence urge upon Your Honours in their final brief that he took all steps that he was able to comply with the law and not to, in any way, allow any crimes to be committed or go undetected or unpunished. And we say this is very far from what the documentation produced at the time reveals. Your Honours, finally, can we ask that Your Honours look at a very short video-clip P0265. This is Zupljanin and others being interviewed on January the 12th, 1993, about the -- effectively the security situation. One of the other people in the studio is, in fact, then the assistant minister, Tomo Kovac. And I think Your Honours will see a quick clip of what he looked like in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there we see Zupljanin saying exactly what the Prosecution say, is that the police did, as they say they did, they tasked which normally would have been outside their responsibility, which would be the guarding of camps, where they say this was a necessity because of the -- as they put it, the citizens are to be protected on specific territory. Your Honours, thank you very much for the extra time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this morning I want to begin by talking about communications, a matter that's been discussed a lot in this courtroom, or more often in Courtroom III, I guess, during the past couple of years. On the screen, the first slide I want to show you lists some of the various means and modes of communication that were available to the accused and to RS MUP in 1992. They had telephones, fax machines, teletype and teleprinters for sending coded communications, had short-wave and ultra short-wave radios. When necessary, they could use human beings as couriers. There were frequent face-to-face meetings and collegiums at both the headquarters level, the CSB levels, and in addition to the MUPs country-wide communication system there were two other republic-wide communication systems that could be used by the MUP. One was the army system, once the VRS was in place, and there was also the Ministry of Defence which had its republican -- republic communications centre. You'll recall Mr. Vukovic who worked there testified about that system that was primarily for the use of the republic level political organs but they had the means to communicate with all the municipalities. He testified that all three of those communication providers assisted each other from time to time as needed and as necessary. I just give you one example of the use of an alternative communications network. Mr. Tutus testified at page 7712 about a time when he needed to get in touch with the minister. The communications system in Banja Luka was having some problems on that occasion, so he went to the centre, and reading from line 6 on that page he said: "I couldn't directly contact the minister so I went to the communications centre. I asked the operator to connect me with the minister through other means of communication that Republika Srpska had at its disposal at the time, and he did put me through to General Tolimir through some sort of military communications. And from Tolimir, I asked the connection to Stanisic. Ten minutes later or less I got feedback from General Tolimir that Mr. Stanisic agreed with my decision." That is just one example of the alternative means being used. Vukovic's testimony has more detail, and that's at transcript 1761 through 24, 17655 and 17691 to 92. In addition, you've heard how part of the problem was that the post telegraph and telephone system, the PTT system, was disrupted because of the war and the division of territory. You have in evidence one reference pertaining to that system. In Exhibit P1755, General Mladic's notebook, regarding a meeting on the 31st of July, he receives a report from the chief of communications for his Herzegovina Corps. At page 393 and 394 of both the English and the B/C/S, in e-court, the chief reports a communications system is fully operational. And on 394 he reports that the PTT system of the SAOH, the Serbian Autonomous Region of Herzegovina, is better now than before the war. That's the report on the 31st of July. Now, if we could go to the next slide. If you really need or want to do some more research into the state communications, there are several sources that you can look at. They're various annual reports; VRS MUP annual report, P625 [Realtime transcript read in error "P265"] we'll look more at that in a minute; P624 [Realtime transcript read in error "P264"] is the annual report for Banja Luka CSB; the testimony of the various communication witnesses, Mr. Vukovic, I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hannis, just for the sake of record, you said "625" and "624" and it was recorded "264" and "265." I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I think it's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's correct. I did think I said and intended to say 625 and 624. The communication witnesses, including Mr. Vukovic, were Mr. Kuzunovic, from RS MUP at the top level; Mr. Pejic, who worked in the CSB in Sarajevo; Mr. Rakovic in CSB Banja Luka; Mr. Jankovic from Prijedor; and Mr. Raljic from Kotor Varos. A couple of the log-books, I have spared you all of the pain in bringing any log-books and trying to discuss them today. But, again, I would encourage you to have a look at them. P1428 is the communications log-book that was initially used in Vraca by Mr. Kuzunovic at the MUP headquarters level, and then later you heard that very same notebook was taken over and used as the log-book for CSB Sarajevo by Mr. Pejic. That one, if you would look at some of the testimony of Mr. Pejic we walked through several of the links. And P1025 is the Prijedor log-book that we spent a lot of time with Mr. Jankovic. Intercepts were another means of communication and you have a number of intercepts in evidence. I think the Defence all along and still in their brief try to argue about the weight of that evidence and still have an issue with them. I think Your Honours should be well satisfied by know that that evidence is something reliable. A number of those had been confirmed by the actual speakers. Many of them are self-authenticating to a certain extent just based on their contents. The caller comes. You hear him ask, May I speak with Mr. Stanisic. Someone comes on the phone and says he is Mr. Stanisic. They have a conversation about something we know about from either other telephone conversations or other documents that make sense in the context of date and the events that are going on. And we think you can rely on those. Collegiums we have six RS MUP collegiums. July, August, September, October and November, and a reference to the one in December. We don't have the actual minutes to that but we have documents referring to it both before it occurred and after it occurred. And you can see from those collegiums that there must have been other communications prior to the meetings. You can't get a group of people together unless the meeting is scheduled and people are informed that they need to come and attend, and the fact that they did occur indicates prior communications and the contents of the collegium. You see what they're talking about. You see that they've had prior communications about those kinds of things. Assembly sessions, the Bosnian Serb Assembly met several times in 1992. Can you see from those lengthy conversations in some of the assembly sessions that there's been a lot of communication, not only among the delegates but with other people outside the assembly, including police and army personnel. And, likewise, government sessions. I think there some 60 government sessions in evidence. We may not have all 60 but there are approximately that many. Mr. Stanisic was a member of the government as the minister of interior in 1992. He often attended. When he's not present, his absence is generally noted and one of his representatives is attending; I think on one occasion, Mr. Kovac, Mr. Njegus, various peoples whose names you will recognise as members of the MUP headquarters. Now, we have more details about the communication in our final trial brief in paragraphs 881 through 886. I refer you there for further detail. And if we could go to the next slide. This is P625, the MUP draft annual report. There are two sections that deal with communications. This first one was entitled: Reporting and informing. This, I believe, has more to do with the -- the section of the MUP that dealt with analysis where they send out requests for information or they sent out questionnaires. They received information back and prepared reports. You see from this excerpt taken from pages 22 and 23 of the English in P625, 31 and 35 in the B/C/S, talks about a number of reports that were prepared during the year. And concerning reporting and informing, some 4170 dispatches were sent to the centres and other organs, and about 4400 were received. Now, this is different from the next slide. This is also in the report. Section 3 was about task and duties of communications and cryptographic data protection. You see the numbers here of dispatches sent and received. In addition to the dispatches, it notes that: "Some 9.585 short-wave radio connections were established from the communications centre base alone ..." Again, this is for the period from April through December 1992. Related to that, we should look at the next slide which is the report for the period from 4 April 1992 to 31 April 1992 for the CSB in Banja Luka. And, again, we'll have two different types of communication and reporting. This first one you have on the slide is the cryptographic data protection and communications system. There were a total of 15.981 dispatches received. That includes both the open and closed or coded dispatches, if my math is right. And something near 14.339 were sent. That's a total of both the open and closed dispatches. In addition to that, it notes that they forwarded 2.297 dispatches. You may recall evidence we heard where, on occasion, for example, I think Zvornik was one, where they were not able to communicate with Sarajevo but they were able to communicate with Bijeljina and they requested that Bijeljina forward dispatch to Sarajevo. I believe that this is what was happening in Banja Luka as well. Sometimes they were requested to forward a dispatch that another unit could not connect with at the time. Go to the next slide. Still in P624, the report for Banja Luka CSB. This about task and assignments concerning analysis and information. I think this is the same that was seen in the MUP headquarters report concerning reporting and informing. Total of 111 reports on security issues were submitted to government organs in municipalities. 206 reports were submitted to the army. 632 reports to the MUP. I assume that means MUP headquarters from CSB Banja Luka. And the bottom paragraph you see the centre's professional council held regular meetings. This is the collegium on the CSB level; an example of communications occurring at that level. If we could go one more slide and just want to touch briefly on some of the Defence claims regarding communications that were made during the trial. There was a reference to the extreme drop off in the number of dispatches as a reflection of the difficulties the RS MUP was having in 1992. And I think Mr. Kuzunovic was the first one that this was put to that, Gee, before the war wasn't there about 300.000 dispatches a year, and here in this reports you only see 4.000 or 8.000, some much smaller number. First of all, we don't have a document reflecting what the number was in 1991 or the first three months in 1992, we only have that Bare testimony. In addition you remember before the split, the MUP of Bosnia covered more than the 70 or so municipalities that we eventually had in the RS. There was something in the neighbourhood I think of 110 or 109 municipalities is the evidence about the total territory. In addition, I think Mr. Pejic is the one who told us that before the war, there were all kinds of dispatches that were sent that simply did not get sent during the war time for some pretty obvious reasons. If you're engaged in a war it's probably not worth your time or effort to be sending out a dispatch to try and locate a stolen bicycle or a car or other kinds of, sort of, routine police business that is done during peacetime. In addition, there were obviously fewer policemen working in the RS MUP because it was a smaller area, fewer personnel, so they're fewer policemen to actually be doing police work that requires reporting and sending dispatches about. And for security reasons Mr. Pejic, I think, also mentioned this: That there were more comms, more communications, done outside the dispatch system. You've seen from some of the intercepts that the speakers were aware that oftentimes they were being eavesdropped on. You heard the expressions of concern about sending dispatches by fax for security reasons, and so much more of the communication occurred either by face-to-face communication or outside the dispatch system. Mr. Pejic at transcript page 12129 and 1230 -- 12130. Before the war, dispatches that went from the SUP toward the centres and police stations could include 100 or 200 dispatches in a packet because dispatches are used to inform relevant institutions of all security relevant matters such as stolen vehicles, whereas during war-time those wouldn't be so numerous. He went on to say: "But it was expected the number of dispatches about security relevant events become much greater but such information was, however, mostly transmitted by phone or in direct contact between the officers, and dispatches were used only when other means of communication were not possible. I believe that the officers in charge compensated for that through telephone communications or other types of communications." Second remark of the 30 per cent increase to be expected during the war was a suggestion I think initially put by Mr. Zecevic to one or more of the communication witnesses. We never heard a basis for that estimate, and I fail to see what that could possibly be based on. None of the witnesses had been in the experience of going through a -- a war in their former country and comparing the communications with peacetime communications. It seems like a completely wild, out-of-the air guess and has no basis that you can rely on. Finally, completely cut off was a phrase, I think, we heard often from witnesses about the situation regarding communications. I think we're not completely cut off. People got around. Mr. Stanisic and all the RS big shots, Mr. Karadzic, Koljevic, Krajisnik, Mrs. Plavsic, Trbojevic and Djeric, including the RS Assembly members were able to travel around. They all showed up in Banja Luka on May 12th for the Assembly session, and you will see from the Assembly sessions they met at various locations throughout the RS in 1992. I guess one of the best examples I would refer you to in -- it was generally like for the police and communications in 1992 come from the testimony of ST-179 at T7472 through 76. They basically said at the beginning of the conflict they used couriers for communication. By June, the telephones were working. By August, teleprinter and telegraph was working. He also said that the SJB chiefs had periodic, at least monthly meetings with their CSB chief, including one that was held at the hotel Kosude [phoen] where Mr. Stanisic had his office at the time. And at those meetings the SJB chiefs would regularly inform the CSB chief about events and steps that needed to be taken and that the CSB chief would draw conclusions and forward them to the minister, Mr. Stanisic. Your Honours, I guess that's where I want to sum up. Yes, there were problems with communications and there were difficulties. But one thing I'd like about communications witnesses, generally, compared to politicians or policemen or generals from the army in this kind of case is that the communication guys are engineers, and their job is to figure out how to make things work, not to have a discussion about whether it should work or who is going to be in charge of it working, whatever. They try to solve problems and that's what they did. When the telephone didn't work, then they tried to set up a radio-relay connection. They used couriers, they delivered messages face to face. It is obvious that communications were occurring. Things weren't ideal. They never are. But can see from the totality of the evidence, the people who needed to know got the information, maybe not as quickly as they would have liked in the ideal circumstance, but it was not the situation the Defence would have you believe that some kind of prehistoric situation with no communications or post-apocalyptic situation where everything has been destroyed and you have to resort to signal flares and smoke signs. Communications worked. Now let me talk about Mr. Stanisic, unless there's a particular question. Now I want to talk about Mico Stanisic, minister of the interior for the RS MUP in 1992, and back for a while in 1994. First slide, character evidence. In his brief, Mr. Stanisic has put character into evidence, and I would point out that the good character is not a defence to the charges, might be a factor you consider for mitigation in sentencing, but it is not a Defence to charges. Good people sometimes do bad things. But, indeed, the character witnesses cited in the Defence brief at paragraphs 20 and 41 include some folks that I would highly suggest to you are not the most reliable witnesses that have appeared here, including, Mr. Macar, Mr. Planojevic, Mr. Zepinic. And it's odd that Mr. Stanisic refers to Mr. Zepinic as one of his character witnesses, on the one hand, and then when it comes to Mr. Zepinic's evidence, in transcript 5828 through 5832 about the incident where he says Mr. Stanisic pulled a gun or him, they ask you to completely disregard that. But I would say there's other evidence that suggests that Mr. Zepinic may be telling you the truth about that and that it's not out of character for Mr. Stanisic in 1992. We heard some testimony about the loud argument in confrontation between Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Djeric. Djeric talked about that at transcript 2583. You had some partial corroboration that such an event occurred from Trbojevic at transcript 4122 and 23. And a third person, ST-127, at transcript 11912 through 13 told you a detailed example. Reading from line 17 of 11912: "His driver called me up from Jahorina and told me that the minister had ordered me to wait for him in the room where we met last. And I was there. He came. He was extremely angry, furious which surprised me greatly. I was flabbergasted. I entered the room and Mr. Stanisic -- I don't know how to put it. It would be a bad thing for me to say that he shouted or hollered, but it was terrible for a highly educated man in such a high position the way he behaved. I felt like a slave. I didn't dare move. He walked up and down in the room shouting, accusing me of obstructing this or that. And I didn't know what to -- could happen at any moment, and it went on for an hour at least. And I know once it was over, nobody could be found in the neighbouring offices. In those angry outbursts and in issuing threats to me, he went on, and I noticed that he was armed. He had a pistol in a holster and he touched that holster several times, and I didn't know that, what he might be able to do that. I had never seen him like that. And, finally, he said to me extremely angrily that on the following morning I would be out in the trenches with the military somewhere on Mount Jahorina." So three different sources talking about that aspect of his character. And one intercept - this is the next slide I would like to show you - it's a phone call on the 18th of April, 1992, between Minister Stanisic and Radomir Kojic. We'll talk about him a little bit later. And you'll see that Mr. Kojic is informing him about another individual named Zoka who has arrested certain people, and they made an agreement that those people would be brought to Vraca and handed over. He says: "They can beat them. They can do whatever they fucking want. And then we will move them because we have no space here." Mr. Stanisic's reaction was: Fine. Let me go to the next slide. The Defence pointed out that Mr. Stanisic co-operated with the OTP. Again, if anything that goes perhaps to mitigation for sentencing if there's conviction, but from a reading of the totality of the interview it's our position that the co-operation was more in the nature of an effort to try and make the case against him go away. We believe a fair reading of the interview shows that he was less than fully forthcoming. And if you would take the time, Your Honours, I would encourage you to look at P2309 at pages 26 through 35 in the English to give you a little flavour of the interview. Mr. Tieger, the Prosecutor at the time, who was asking him about the minutes of the 11 July collegium in Belgrade and the subsequent 17 July analysis and conclusions taken from that meeting. In particular, asking him about what Mr. Zupljanin had said about the numerous Muslims who had been rounded up by the army and the Crisis Staff who were trying to round up as many as possible and putting them in these undefined camps under miserable conditions. And in the -- in the conversation, the way the questions and answers went, I think illustrates that he was not really co-operating. He quibbled with Mr. Tieger's reference to the number of people being detained as many, many, and insisted on a number. When Mr. Tieger suggested that those people were victims, he said: "Who do you mean?" Mr. Tieger had to clarify: "I mean those Muslims that you agreed were being held in those camps without any criminal charges against them." Please have a look. A couple of other instances in the interview I want to refer to just to try and illustrate the point. Next slide, please. He was asked if he was involved in any operational aspects of what the MUP was doing during the time he was at Vrace which you will recall was in the first few weeks of the war. His answer was: "The minister is not involved in the operation aspect. It's a minister's duty to provide guide-lines for the work of MUP and to adopt legal regulations." But, what do you actually do while I was at Vrace, you will see was more in the nature of some operational work. If we can go to the next slide. There are a series of intercepts. I'm not going to put them all up in the interests of my limited time but you have him speaking directly with Mr. Karisik who was head of the RS MUP special unit. The first instance on 1 July, he tells them to destroy those targets. The next day he is telling, Take them down, screw them. Do not take any risks, just take them down. Again, get down those targets. And the last one is not a conversation with Mr. Stanisic but with Karisik and Mr. Kusmuk who at the time was the assistant minister for police administration. Mr. Karisik is requesting Kusmuk to get a particular tam vehicle with an anti-aircraft gun. Mr. Kusmuk advising that can only be done with the approval or permission of the minister, so the minister is involved in the operational aspects and the work at that time. Next slide. Also in the interview, there was a discussion about the relationship between the minister and his subordinates and how there were difficulties caused by the political authorities, the Crisis Staffs. And Mr. Stanisic said all the time up until their dissolution, the Serb Autonomous District which happened in September, the head of the CSBs as well as the heads of the police stations did not merely hold the position of head of CSBs or police stations, they were also members of Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies. And a little further down, he goes on to say, And because the minister did not have de facto jurisdiction during that period of time - here's my emphasis added - you cannot find a single order of the head of the CSBs or the head of the police stations referring to any order of mine or any of my assistants between April and September. You may remember off the top of your head we have many orders of the minister and from some of his assistants that are referred to specifically in orders of the CSBs and referred on down to the SJBs. We'll show you a few. If we could go two slides over. 1D73 is an exhibit that is the 25 April order from Minister Stanisic numbered 01-25 delegating his authority regarding appointment of certain personnel to CSB chiefs. We have in evidence P384 which is Mr. Zupljanin forwarding that order -- which referring to order specifically in his appointment of Mr. Vrucinic as the chief of Sanski Most SJB. It's also cited by the Doboj chief, Mr. Bjelosevic, in 1D464, his appointment of the deputy for CSB, Mr. Milan Savic, who you will recall associated with the Mice. P1004 is Mr. Stanisic's order of May 4th, and again you'll see that that was forwarded by Mr. Zupljanin, referred to by number, and it shows up in the Prijedor log-book. 1D58 is Mr. Stanisic's 7 July order to take measures against MUP members who commit criminal acts, again cited by Mr. Zupljanin, forwarded to Prijedor appearing in the log-books. It's also cited by CSB chief, Krsto Savic, and forwarded to his subordinate SJBs. Those are a few examples of the orders from Mr. Stanisic between April and September. So clearly, that statement in his interview was not true. Next slide. This is only a small one. This was when Mr. Tieger was asking Mr. Stanisic about the events when the 400 or so prisoners from Bratunac were brought to Pale. You may recall that testimony. And Mr. Stanisic claimed that he didn't know about that, that he was out of town. The evidence indicates this occurred on the 15th and 16th of May. Mr. Tieger pressed Mr. Stanisic for information about where he was, where he had been during the time. He said: "Well, sir, I just wasn't there and I should disclose this thing during the procedure of presenting evidence." We don't know where he was. We know that on 12th of May he was in Banja Luka. We see him at the parade, the police parade, the day that the Assembly met. We know that on the 15th of May he was writing his order creating war units; 1D146. And we know on the 16th of May he was writing up a follow-up order about reporting about war crimes against Serb victims. But we don't know where he was. Skipina says that he did tell Stanisic about the Bratunac group the day after they were transported, but no further information. Finally, if we could go to the next slide on the interview. One more. Again, this is when Mr. Tieger was asking about the July 11th collegium. Mr. Stanisic said: "Mr. Tieger, since they are documents in the concept of my Defence hinges on the documents I would prefer not to discuss them at this time ... I had some documents that I would prefer not to disclose ... you need to understand the Defence hinges on a certain strategy ... keeping undisclosed in keeping with rules of undisclosing documents since I am accused." Now, Your Honours, the Defence pointed out in the brief that under the statute in the Celebici judgement, it's inappropriate to comment on a defendant's non-testifying. However, I found no Tribunal jurisprudence dealing with the situation we have here where the accused has chosen to waive his right and speak. His interview in 2007 was done pursuant to the Rules. He was cautioned before each and every session. His lawyer was present with him and so he did speak about a number of matters, but he spoke selectively. And we say based on jurisdiction from other domestic jurisdictions, US, Australia, elsewhere, that, in that case, when a defendant partially waives his right, he cannot use that as a sword. I see Mr. Zecevic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- Your Honours, I have to object to this, because it is -- I mean, perhaps I will give the reasons later, but I think this line is quite in contrast with the jurisprudence of this Tribunal; because Tribunal jurisprudence is very clear about the fact that there is -- and the Statute for that purpose, that the accused cannot be compelled to testify in a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's an argument, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We -- we hear Mr. Hannis, and we would consider it, just like all the other arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This may again raise the issue Ms. Korner spoke about before that there may be a request for some further submissions on particular legal matters that we can outside of the framework of the argument, but I did want to point this out; because we think that in these circumstances where a defendant has made some statements and made certain assertions about what he has or what he might show and then he doesn't, that we can comment on that to you, and that's something you can consider, at least related to the -- to his credibility or to what weight to give the statement that he did make. The one US Supreme Court case I would cite to you is Rylander versus United States, 103 Supreme Court 1548, a case in 1983. The holding there was in the US. Our constitutional privilege then applies to the fifth amendment, the protection against self-incrimination. Rylander held that an accused could not convert the privilege from a shield against compulsory self-incrimination, which it was intended to be. You cannot convert that into a sword whereby a claimant asserting the privilege would be freed from adducing proof in support of a burden which would otherwise have been here. And, yes, there are several cases from Australia and England, but I want to move on to more factual matters. All right. If we could go to the slide on background. Four brief topics I want to touch concerning background raised by the Defence: SDS, arming, council of ministers, national security council. Defence have argued that Mr. Stanisic was not a member of the SDS. We think the evidence shows that he was. If he wasn't a card-carrying member, he was certainly a -- an important affiliate, associate, supporter, and fan of the SDS. We would ask you to look at P883. This is referred to in the Defence -- in Mr. Stanisic's brief at paragraph 34 pointing out the mistranslation, originally referred to a list of people as members of the SDS. And he pointed out that the correct translation should be "cadre of the SDS." I'm not sure how that helps. My understanding of "cadre" refers to members of an organisation who are the core members, the key members around whom you would build your group; comes from, as I understand, the Latin quadro, meaning square. So the fact is that Mr. Stanisic is listed as being part of the cadre of the SDS holding a position in the ministries. You can also look at P1467 and P522, which shows his involvement or connection with SDS activities. 522, his -- his being listed as a member of the Crisis Staff of the SDS for the city of Sarajevo. And being assigned a task that arises from the December 19th instructions, the Variant A and B instructions. He claims he never saw it, but he is listed and assigned a task that would be appropriate for him in his position at the time. P1467 is 25 September 1991 decision of the SDS appointing a regionalisation staff and naming Mr. Stanisic to that. And, I guess, the best argument is whether he is a member or not he is certainly a supporter, and that's found in a statement he made at the Assembly on the 23rd and 24th of November. It's from P4100 [sic] at pages 50 -- yes. This -- he says: "He's here to stress this to you as well that I, as a man, have followed policies of the SDS Presidency and our deputies in the former state. I have always followed these policies. Those who want to separate me from them, I will always be with them until it is shown that their wishes an intentions differ from those of the people." That was on the 23rd and 24th of November, 1992. Let me talk a little bit about arming. The best example of this is also a comment from an Assembly session but this one comes from his colleague, Mr. Mandic. If we could go to the next slide. This is an Assembly session on the 30 and 31st of December, 1993, P1990, English page 164, B/C/S page 197. Mr. Mandic is speaking: "Vito," meaning Zepinic here, I believe, "Vito and Delimustafic, it is true gentleman that they want to put me in prison. And do you know why? Because together with Stanisic I pulled out 560 Hecklers from the MUP to Romanija and distributed them to Sokolac, Rogatica, Han Pijesak and Pale." You've heard other evidence or references to Mr. Stanisic and arming. Council of ministers. Mr. Stanisic was a member of the council of ministers. Initially a minister without portfolio. Oh I see in the transcript at line -- page 23, line 2, it says "P4100." It should be "P400," is the exhibit number for that Assembly session in November. Now, as a member of the ministerial council, Mr. Stanisic attended the very first meeting held on 11 January. You'll see this in document P268. And at that session, if we could go to the next slide, oh, I see it's on the screen now. You'll see that the conclusion under number 2 about the priorities for the council of ministers included the defining of ethnic territory, establishment of government organs in the territory, and the economic disempowerment of the current authorities in the Socialist Republic of BiH. If we could go to the next slide. On the next page of the document it mentions that a working group is going to be composed, and Mr. Stanisic is responsible for the work of the group. Even though Mr. Zepinic is in the group and Mr. Zepinic is the highest ranking Serb in the joint MUP at the time, Mr. Stanisic is designated to be responsible for the work of this group which is to deal with issues regarding the organisation and scope of national security and frame a concept about it. You'll see shortly thereafter in, I think, the next meeting of the council of ministers that they come up with a proposal for the creation of a national security council which, indeed, is what happened. And the minister of the interior was an ex officio member of the national security council, and Mr. Stanisic didn't work with that body. The Defence in their brief say that, Well, the national security council wasn't really a body with any authority. It didn't have any executive authority. It was only advisory. I think if you review all the evidence that it was something more than a mere advisory body; in effect, it acted in the place of a Presidency during that interim in the early part of 1992 before a RS Presidency was actually created. On that, I would refer you to the testimony of Mr. Djokanovic, later on a republic War Commissioner, at one time minister for youth and sports I believe was his title in the RS. His testimony at page 3569 and 70, he is speaking about in the first few weeks of the war he was at Vrace. And he was present at a meeting in late April or early May where Mr. Karadzic was in Vrace. Mr. Stanisic was at this meeting. He believed that Mr. Karisik was there as well. And he said at line 1 on 3570: "The people there were interested in the Serb side cutting the city in two. In other words, to divide the city from Vrace towards Skenderija by the football pitch. And I think someone mentioned this to Mr. Karadzic, and Karadzic replied that he could not issue and order to that effect. That is something that would have to be decided by the council for national security." So here you have early discussion on what turned out to be one of the six strategic objectives, dividing the city of Sarajevo, and Mr. Karadzic indicating that that was something that he couldn't decide but it would have to be decided by the council of national security. This is in late April or early May. Next slide, please. A plan to split the BiH MUP. Ms. Korner has spoken about this during his presentation on the introduction. And as already mentioned, indication of this can be found -- another indication about the fact that there was a plan I think is reflected in some of the year-in reports from various MUP SJBs. I would urge you to look at the Prijedor SJB report, P689. Mr. Drljaca's reporting about the covert preparations outside the station in early 1992. Covertly forming Serbian police stations and arming Serbian personnel. P348 is the Zvornik annual report. It also referred to the illegal activity of Serbian personnel in the MUP in making plans for a potential separate Serbian MUP. And you may recall with Mr. Kovac we showed him some of the award nominations that were put forward for him talking about his involvement in illegal activity in arming the Serbs and making preparations for creating a new Serbian MUP. It's almost as though it is a point of pride in these reports. And, again, that counters a Defence argument that there was no plan and that they only were trying to go along with Cutileiro. Don't make sense. Next, Stanisic's authority. Clearly, Mr. Stanisic had the power to appoint and replace CSB and SJB chiefs. You heard Mr. Kovac talk about that. You've seen his order from 25 April in 1D73. Mr. Olmsted will talk about this in more detail in his presentation. Regarding disbanding the specials and reducing the reserve, the primary document is 1D176. And related to this issue of reducing the reserve force and removing criminals, there's been some debate about what Mr. Stanisic said in the Assembly session, again on the 22nd -- or 23rd and 24th of November, 1992. Mr. Zecevic pointed out that there initially was a mistake in the interpretation but I want to go back to the document. It is P400 at page 17 in the English, and 17, 18 in the B/C/S. Can we have the next slide. Oh, I'm sorry, I'm not ready for that. But it was pointed out that the correct interpretation was: "They took in thieves and criminals, because I tell you not a single doctor picked up a rifle to defend his country, not a single intellectual. Out priority, our intentions were good and maybe that's where we went wrong." I urge Your Honours to look closely at Mr. Stanisic's entire speech in that section of the Assembly session. And read in context, we believe, "they" is referring to himself and the MUP. Now, Mr. Mandic, good friend of Mr. Stanisic, at least in the context of this case, when he testified, went out of his way, I would say, not in response to a question that was put to him, but at transcript 9564, he volunteered and said, Can I just add something, Judge? He volunteered that they didn't mean RS MUP or Mico Stanisic but, instead, referred to powerful people who invited in the paramilitaries from outside. Well, we say that doesn't make sense in the context of this, and one reason I say that is based on another remark attributed to Mr. Stanisic closer in time to his 27 July order about removing criminals. And that can be found in Mladic's notebook, P1755, at pages 373 to 375. If we could show the next slide, please. Very same day that Mr. Stanisic had issued that order, 27 July, he and Mr. Trbojevic, deputy prime minister, had a meeting with Mr. Mladic. And Stanisic is noted as saying: "I had to take everyone into the police." "I had to take everyone into the police." "... but the army has now taken over the lines. We are now in a position to choose policemen." That's consistent with the interpretation that what he was saying in the Assembly in November 1992 was that, yes, in the beginning they had to take criminals and thieves into the police because there was a war on, basically. If we could go onto the next slide. Noted in the same meeting, again, still Mr. Stanisic speaking apparently. He said: "I sent an order this morning that within five days on placing a whole section of forces within the competence of the army." That's a reference to his 1D176 order. And he is noted as saying: "The minister of interior ... has sole jurisdiction in its territory." Now, I want to play a video, Your Honour, if I have time. It's about, I don't know, a minute and a half before the break. And before we start the video I just want to ask Your Honours to take note of what Mr. Stanisic is wearing around his neck in -- not this video. No. Sorry. Yes, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can see the subtitles. I don't know if you can hear the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic with members of special unit. The first one was Mr. Karisik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, am I missing something when you asked us to take note of what he was wearing around his neck?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning, I don't know if you were able to see what he was wearing around his neck. We can go back to it, but I would indicate it appears to be an Orthodox cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, I notice that. But the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the reason I bring that to your attention, Your Honour, is that the Defence in their final trial brief portray essentially Mr. Stanisic as too nice a guy to have even thought about these crimes or doing any of these kind of crimes, and they pointed out to his remarks on the 30th of March in Sokolac, when he announced that, From today, we have our own Serbian MUP, and in the Assembly on 27th of March when he was selected as the minister of the interior. I think on both of those occasions he made remarks to the effect that he wanted to have a professional police organisation and not one that was related to politics, and that he wanted one that would do its job of protecting all the people of all nationalities. Now, the point I'm trying to make is: Here's the minister of the interior purporting to be the representative -- the protector of people of all ethnicities. In the context of this conflict that was ongoing, what he is wearing, I would assert to you, is something that would not give comfort to the non-Serbs. That's not a standard issue for the police. And it seemed to me that there's a message to be conveyed, just certainly a message that would have been received by the non-Serbs viewing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it time for our first break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, now -- we've just seen Mr. Stanisic and his special unit under Milenko Karisik, and I do want to talk briefly about the special units. Under the Law on Internal Affairs for the RS MUP, Article 36 was the provision that gave the minister the power to create special units. And we have evidence in this case that Mr. Karisik's special unit was under the direct authority of Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Planojevic testified about that at transcript 16404. We've had other witnesses indicate that and other documents that reflect it. But I also want to talk about Dusko Malovic. He was head of the special police platoon, sometimes referred to as the Sokolac Platoon. We say the evidence shows that this group was also under the direct authority of Minister Stanisic. Exhibit P1422 is a 15 June 1992 document, an order from Mr. Stanisic to Mr. Malovic's unit, the Sokolac unit of the special police, to carry out mobilisation of conscripts. And you've seen a number of payroll documents concerning Mr. Malovic's units. Mico Davidovic testified at transcript 13606 about Mr. Malovic and his unit being under the authority of the minister. We've had a lot of debate, I guess, between me and Defence counsel about whether or not Malovic and his unit were responsible for personal security of the minister. We have had some evidence about that. Mr. Planojevic in his suspect interview with the OTP had indicated that's what he did, but when Mr. Planojevic came to testify he backed off that testimony. And I think you'll recall, I went through that with him in his statement about how he first came to mention it. It wasn't in response to a question. He volunteered it, which is more consistent with it being genuine. We think his change of testimony was because he was here in front of Mr. Stanisic and that drove the change. You should also look at Mr. Kovac's statement to the Bijeljina prosecutor's office, investigating the murder of the three Muslim families in September of 1992. I'll talk more about that in a minute. Let me move to the Bijeljina murders. Next slide, please. I know this is not a charged incident in the case, but we think it's necessary to talk about it because it reflects on matters of credibility, regarding Mr. Stanisic and other witnesses in the case. It also relates to his connection with the Malovic unit, which ties in with the failure to punish certain individuals and to take actions. And so let me talk about it briefly. Mr. Stanisic has worked very hard to have any connection between him and that event removed or obscured. Mico Davidovic testified at transcript 13552 through 54 and 13604 through 07, as well as in his 92 ter statement, P1557.01 at paragraphs 151 and 152. Malovic generally admitted that his unit had done that crime. Davidovic told you that he had a meeting with Mr. Stanisic after he, Davidovic, had spoken with the OTP on -- on other matters. And Mr. Stanisic asked him if he had said anything about that event. Reading from Davidovic's transcript, 13552: "On one occasion, I met with Mr. Stanisic in Sremska Mitrovica and Stanisic had some questions about why I talked to the investigators of the Tribunal, whether he was also interesting to them, whether I had given any statements, and I said, Yes, I talked to them. They also ask about him in that context, his activities concerning the disarming of paramilitaries in Zvornik, and other places was also discussed. And as far as this family from Bijeljina is concerned, I said that question had not been asked. And then he said, Please don't place me in that context. Because he doesn't want to get involved and he doesn't want me to place him in any context related to that," and that's the first time this family was mentioned with him. He goes on talking about meeting with Dusko Malovic in Belgrade sometime after the event, asking him, who killed those people there. And Malovic told him that Drago Vukovic, the head of secret police of state security in Bijeljina, had ordered it. And shortly after that conversation Mico Stanisic and Frenki Simatovic arrived. This was in Belgrade at the Bosanska Vija [phoen] and Stanisic -- and -- and Davidovic left shortly after that. Now, this was public knowledge at the time. You heard the testimony that the Radical Party, headed by Mirko Blagojevic in Bijeljina had put out a press release about the murders and suggesting that it had been committed by Dusko Malovic and his unit. It's interesting to note also that eight days later, eight days after the murder on the 3rd of October there was a collegium of the RS MUP in Bijeljina presided over by Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Kovac was at that meeting, and Mr. Kovac is listed as having briefed the group on the security situation. Now, I asked him when he testified if he recalled having informed the group about the murders, and I don't have his precise answer in front of me. Please refer to the transcript. But I think the gist was he didn't recall. If he knew and if he knew whether or not he had said anything about it. It's hard to imagine that the murder of three Muslim families, 25 some people including women and children happening in a town like Bijeljina at that time and having been mentioned in the press, was not something that would have been part of the security briefing eight days later in Bijeljina. And I even asked Mr. Davidovic a question about whether he had an opinion as to whether it was possible that the minister did not know about it. And Judge Hall rightly admonished me that I was really asking him to speculate, and I -- I took -- I took his suggestion because he said that maybe what I needed to do was raise it later. Transcript page 13607. Judge Hall: "We have the evidence of the publicity of this. We have the evidence of the fact that the number one accused was a minister at the time, and it is probably an inference, a reasonable inference that you would, at the appropriate time, invite the Chamber to draw, but I think that's as far as can you take it now with the questions for this witness. And I said: "I will take your point, Your Honour. I will save that for submissions later. That's my submission now and all the evidence -- I think it is a reasonable reference to draw. Thank you." Also, related to that, Mr. Stanisic made a statement to the Bijeljina prosecutor's office that was investigating the case. In 2003, he wrote a statement - it's in Exhibit P1543 at pages 65 to 67 - and in that, he claims he didn't know anything about it until apparently some years later that he had issued an order for Dusko Malovic to be sent to Bijeljina and put at the disposal of Mico Davidovic, head of the public security station, and under the full control of MUP senior officer Tomo Kovac and Cedo Kljajic. Said he never got any information concerning any unlawful activities of the special police platoon or Malovic, and that he was never informed about the incident either in writing or verbally as stipulated in the instructions and he didn't -- he didn't learn about the event until sometime after December 1992 after he had left the MUP. Said, I wish to reiterate the atrocities in this sort, making me especially eager to seek accountability of whoever the perpetrators may be especially if they come from the ranks of those who professionally take care of protecting lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. I do get speedy sometimes. We say he had good reason to know who it was and he didn't take any action. And concerning his version of what happened, you've heard testimony from Mr. Davidovic and Mr. Andan. Mr. Davidovic wasn't head of the public security station. He was already gone from Bijeljina by the end of August. He certainly wasn't there in September, in late September when the murders happened. Mr. Andan confirmed that. Mr. Andan wasn't there either because he had been removed. He had been suspended by Mr. Stanisic's decision on the 9th or 10th of September. You have that document in evidence confirmed by Mr. Kovac. Now, we don't have the information from Mr. Kljajic, but Mr. Kovac also made a statement about those events, and that's in Exhibit P2460 at pages 5 and 6 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S. He says: "On my first arrival at the Bijeljina SJB in September 1992, I found the so-called Dusko Malovic's platoon headed at that time by Malovic, by Malovic's deputy, Kuzunovic, who told me at that time their job was to prior security for MUP Bijeljina SJB buildings. I also know that they had gone a number of times from that location and provided security for Mr. Stanisic while he was moving through the territory. They briefly stayed until November, approximately, when they definitively left the area following Mr. Stanisic's removal. That is everything in the task they carried out that I and the police administration knew about, and I believe that, as far as I know, they weren't receiving any other task, although I did not have any command over them because, as provided by law at that time, they were directly linked to Minister Stanisic and they never set off anywhere without Malovic's order." And it may shed some light on it, P737 is a 30 October interview of Mr. Stanisic in "Javnost" magazine or newspaper. One of the questions that he was asked at page 3 of the English and column 3 on the single page in B/C/S. Question: "Some are inclined to accuse the special units of the Ministry of the Interior of the abuse of power when performing their duties in Bijeljina." Stanisic said: "We're determined to protect our constitutional order and unity of Republika Srpska because we're obliged to do so by the constitution. Anyone who decides to disturb the above mentioned has to be aware that we are categorically going to use all the available legal measures to prevent and defeat such attempts. It is not true that the special unit abused the power in Bijeljina." No question to the report about what abuses are you talking about. He just simply categorically denied. All right. Let me move on briefly to the next slide. Paramilitaries. We have some brief information about that. Mr. Nielson in his expert report talks about the relationship between the RS MUP and paramilitaries in his exhibit 508, paragraphs 361 to 378. Mr. Davidovic told you that Stanisic had an agreement with Arkan about coming to Sarajevo. In exchange further assistance in helping fight, they were allowed to loot and take what they wanted from the area. Regarding paramilitaries in Sarajevo, you also have in evidence information about Seselj's men and some local paramilitaries in Ilidza, including Brne's Chetniks, Brne Gavrilovic. Have a look at Exhibit P646 which is a 6 August report from Ilidza, Tomo Kovac, basically his last day as chief in Ilidza before he went to join MUP headquarters. In it, he is praising the work of volunteers, Serb volunteers, compared to the work of the VRS in Ilidza. And it includes the information about the amount of ammunition that the RS MUP has furnished to those volunteers to help in the fighting. Next slide, please. Camps, detainees, and exchanges. Discussed in our final trial brief at paragraph 648 to 668, in Stanisic's brief, I think he tries to make the claim that he didn't know about this until the July collegium on the 11th in Belgrade. The evidence is clear that he had information to put him on a notice far before that. They knew from the very start on the 6th of April after Vrace had been taken over by Karisik, Mandic, non-Serb cadets had been captured, and Stanisic ordered them interrogated and then to be exchanged for Serb prisoners, including Radomir Kojic, the gentleman who we saw on the intercept earlier in my remarks. This testimony comes from Mr. Skipina at transcript 8300 through 04. On 6 June, you have in evidence P427.07. It is an order from the central exchange commission, the body that was created to deal with exchange of prisoners and dead bodies and other persons. It was directed to those whose employees were securing persons in custody. And if you look at the last page of that exhibit, you'll note that it was sent to the MUP, to CSBs, but it was not sent to the army. So on the 6th of June, at least the exchange commission had the understanding that prisoners were being guarded by the police. On the 10th of June, Exhibit P179.7 [sic], it's a government session. That's .07. It's a government session attended by Minister Stanisic, and during the meeting there's a mention of the Ministry of Justice to report about prisoners with special attention on the treatment of civilian population, all information putting Stanisic on notice about detainees being -- detained in facilities guarded by the police before the 11th of July. Let me go to a new topic. Next slide. A big argument put forward during the Defence case was that Mr. Stanisic couldn't have any effective control over subordinates because of inference from the Crisis Staffs. Talked about the appointment of SJB chiefs. Recall, first of all, how things happened in the beginning. The Variant A and Variant B instructions were issued to the SDS municipal organs. Variant A was for those municipalities where there was a Serb majority, where they were effectively were in power in charge of the municipal assembly. Variant B, to those municipalities where they were a minority and had to set up, basically, a shadow government and work covertly. But those instructions provided for the SDS to include as a member in their Crisis Staffs in the municipality in Variant A to include the chief of police or the commander; because in a Serb majority municipality, one of those two positions would be held by a Serb under the inter-party agreement about division of appointments. In the -- in the Variant B municipalities that was not the case, and the instruction in Variant A and Variant B was to include someone from all the appropriate municipal organs that was a Serb to be in that position so that when the time came of -- came for a take-over, that person could assume the role. That's how some of these SDS-appointed police chiefs came into being. Because when the split happened, and when the MUP, the RS MUP came into being on 30 March, according to Mr. Stanisic's pronouncement in Sokolac, he and the RS MUP wasn't in a position to make appointments all over the board. So that's why they didn't have RS MUP appointees in some municipalities at the beginning. However, the RS MUP could and did replace municipality-appointed or SDS Crisis Staff appointees during 1992. Mr. Bjelosevic told you, Oh, we couldn't do anything about Stevo Todorovic in Bosanski Samac because he was appointed by the local municipal authorities, the Crisis Staff. So he wasn't really a member of the MUP, so we couldn't discipline. We couldn't do anything. That's not -- that's not the case. Mr. Olmsted may speak a little further about this, you have the example in Zvornik. Just after the Yellow Wasps round up the local police chief, I think it was Mr. Veselic, was replaced by the RS MUP, and he was a Crisis Staff or provisional government, or whatever the body was called in Zvornik at the time. He had been appointed by the municipal authorities, no hesitation in replacing him. Article 27 of the Law on Internal Affairs calls for SJBs to execute the regulations pertaining to law and order issued by the municipal authority. So it's agreed that in time of emergency or state of imminent threat of war, the Crisis Staff stands in place of the municipal authority so this provision should be read as applying to them. And, if the Crisis Staff is passing some regulation pertaining to law and order, and we say setting a curfew, maybe ordering the roundup of weapons from suspected individuals who might try and overthrow the government. All those kind of things are regulations pertaining to law and order, and the Law on Internal Affairs says that the police station -- that the SJB is to implement those orders. Mr. Stanisic's final trial brief citations about inference don't really support the point. Have a look at the footnote 600 -- paragraph 600 to 601 and footnotes 1193 to 1195. Those documents don't really stand for the point that they pertain, or that they purport to support. For example, P750 is one of the footnoted documents. That's a document from the War Presidency of Kljuc addressed to Banja Luka; because they have received dispatches that are asking them to set up facilities and accept prisoners who are now being moved out of Manjaca and returned to various local municipalities, and the Kljuc war staff says, We can't do that. We're unable to provide reception centres. We don't meet the basic requirements for that. We're proposing to delay the return until further notice. Or, they are taken over by humanitarian organisations operating in Banja Luka with reception centres at their disposal. It's not -- this is not the Crisis Staff ordering the local police to do anything. It's a request from the Crisis Staff to Banja Luka CSB for relief from something that they don't have the facilities to do. P668 is one of the footnoted documents and it is from Simo Drljaca to Mr. Zupljanin informing him that the Prijedor War Presidency has decided to reduce the number of policemen guarding prisoners in Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska. It notes that the armies refuse to take up that duty, and Mr. Drljaca is requesting that some arrangement be made with the army and saying he cannot -- he cannot implement the Crisis Staff decision. It's not that is he implementing a Crisis Staff decision contrary to what the -- what the MUP wants, he has been requested to implement something and he's not doing it. So this is the exact opposite of the point the Defence is trying to make. It is not the Crisis Staff interfering with the work of the police. Have a look at each of those documents cited for those footnotes I mentioned and see whether they pertain or not. Skip the next slide please, and can we go to P163. Yes. Now, regarding the relationship between the municipal authorities or the regional authorities and the RS MUP, at the Trebinje collegium on 20th August Mr. Stanisic addresses directly. It is in Exhibit P163 at page 8 of the English and pages 10 through 12 of the B/C/S. And this is one of the conclusions pointed out by Mr. Stanisic. Number one: "CSB chiefs and their associates must be and are the representatives of the ministry for the region, which is why they should establish day-to-day co-operation with republican deputies," the Assembly guys from the region, "and other representatives of the regional authorities. SJB chiefs should, in the same manner, establish relations with representatives of the municipal authorities. The reason for this is that we are a professional service protecting the interests of the people, and such an activity and orientation requires direct, daily direct contact with the representatives of a legal authorities." As we've said before relating to the issue of subordination and I would say relating to this issue about relations between the Crisis Staffs and police really doesn't matter. This is a joint criminal enterprise. They're in it together. At that same meeting, Mr. Stanisic also made a remark, that I may be stealing from Mr. Olmsted. If we could look at the next slide in item number 5 said: "When performing their duties, police officers cannot take sides whatever the demands and attempts in this stage of establishing the organs of municipal and republican authority. Their work must be only -- must only be based on the law ... it's the only way to avoid contributing to the instability of a situation in a certain area. In this sense, we must resolutely support each and every one of our members, even when they overstep the exercise of lawful authority to a limited degree." That's reflective of the general attitude that we talked about during the trial in our pleadings. Serbs didn't want to arrest other Serbs for committing crimes against non-Serbs in the context of this conflict. Two or three other brief items. Thank you. Credibility. Next slide, please. You're the Judges of credibility, sat here in the courtroom. You watched everything come in and testify in front of you. You will make those discussions. I suggest to you, in many cases you have to reject substantial portions of the testimony of some individuals because they simply were not credible, not reliable. Talked about Stanisic's interview and reasons that may undermine credibility about portions of that. But I want to mention, in particular, two Defence -- two witnesses: One who actually testified in the Prosecution case, Mr. Mandic, and a Defence witness, Mr. Macar. Mandic -- just one little episode that is reflective, I think. You will see his cross-examination by Ms. Korner. He had testified in the Krajisnik case that regarding his infamous dispatch of 31 March separating the MUP, that in Krajisnik he testified under oath that Mico Stanisic ordered him to send that out. When he came here, after meeting with the Defence, he testified that, Oh no, no, I was wrong, that was a mistake. It wasn't Mico Stanisic. It was Velibor Ostojic, the minister of information, who remind him that the Law on Internal Affairs had been passed on the 23rd of March and was due to come into effect eight days later, and, therefore, because he was a highest ranking Serb in the joint MUP he had a responsibility to send it out and he sent it out. Read that testimony, transcript 9405 through 9409, and see if it's plausible. It's really not. The way he testified about it initially makes much more sense. Mr. Stanisic would have been the one to tell him to do it. Mr. Stanisic, on the 30th of March, had announced, From today, we have our own Serbian MUP in Sokolac. He ended up by saying, Oh, I -- he was on vacation. He wasn't on vacation. He was doing his tour of the autonomous regions announcing the new Serbian group. He was in Sokolac on the 30th. He was on Trebinje on the 31st. We have evidence about that. Mr. Macar wo was a Defence witness, he was biased. He volunteered favourable information on topics where he really had no basis of knowledge to assert the things he claimed. Two short examples about him. One, really, in a non-responsive answer, he took the opportunity to slam Mico Davidovic by saying that he was not a person who, quote, page 23411: "Mr. Davidovic, he had no experience with the crime enforcement or the criminal procedure act. That he had worked as chief of the general crime section in the Tuzla CSB which covered 18 municipalities. He was in charge of 17 plain clothes detectives. He later became the SJB chief in Bijeljina. Then became the chief inspector in the federal SUP in Belgrade and pointing out all those things to him I asked him if that would change his opinion about whether or not he had no experience and asked him if he was willing to withdraw his comments. But when he came to testify here, he then recalled, Oh, no, no, it really wasn't Mr. Zupljanin who did it, it was Mr. Bulic, a dead guy, conveniently, who had told him that. And that when he went to Prijedor, he helpfully added for the Defence that Mr. Drljaca had said, I'm not having anything to do with you because my bosses, which Mr. Macar explained he understood to mean municipal authority, didn't tell me anything about it. Well, they wouldn't have told have told him anything about it because his municipal bosses wouldn't have known about it. The whole store about Zupljanin forgetting to send the document and the snub doesn't hold up. You saw the kind of man Mr. Macar was and the position he held. It doesn't make sense that he would have suffer as snub like that without having gone to Zupljanin right away to tell him about his subordinate acting that way or reporting it -- he claims he reported it but we have no document. We found no document. He sat on the collegium with Mr. Drljaca in 1994, never raised anything about it.
