utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, ordinarily the police play a central role in the protecting of citizens of a country. As Drago Borovcanin testified: "In every government there are some ministries which are the most important, among them is always the Ministry of Interior, which is in charge of maintaining law and order and protecting citizens and their property." That's transcript page 6828. During periods of ethnic conflict, the police role in protecting citizens and, in particular, those susceptible to persecution is crucial. Tomislav Kovac acknowledged this, referring to the unlawful imprisonment and mistreatment of non-Serbs at detention facilities throughout the RS. He admitted: "According to the law and according to the hierarchy, we, that is, RS MUP, were the strongest structure within the state; and, therefore, our legal and our ethical duty and obligation was to prevent these occurrences." Transcript page 27151. While the VRS had the responsibility not to engage in activities that unlawfully harmed the citizens of the former BiH, the RS MUP was unique among the Serb forces in that they bore the affirmative duty under the law to do everything in their power to protect the population. Under Article 42 of the RS Law on Internal Affairs, this affirmative duty of the police applied: "At all times, regardless of whether they're on duty or whether such a duty is part of a special assignment," and, "even when their life is endangered." Amidst the endemic and systematic crimes that were comitted against the Muslims, the Croats and other non-Serbs in the territory of the RS from the onset of the indictment period, the police should have dedicated their attention and resources to protecting the non-Serb population. This, the evidence shows, they did not do. The most blatant evidence of the failure of the police to protect the non-Serb population was their direct participation in the crimes commit the against that population as described yesterday by Mr. Demirdjian. Another important aspect of the police failure to protect was their failure to investigate, arrest and punish Serb perpetrators of crimes against the non-Serb population. And this is what I will address. The evidence shows that the police stood at the threshold of the criminal justice system. It was their duty to conduct the initial investigation of a crime, to identify and arrest perpetrators, to preserve evidence, and to initiate the criminal proceedings by filing a criminal report with the prosecutor that was supported by sufficient proof of that crime. Even after filing a criminal report, the police remained an integral part of the criminal justice process. The prosecutor and court depended upon the police to conduct searches, to locate and bring in witnesses, to secure evidence and crime scenes, and to conduct forensic examinations, and where there was evidence of additional crimes, to file supplemental criminal reports regarding those crimes. As the former Sanski Most prosecutor, Delic testified, if the police did not perform their role: "The criminal procedures could not be completed." Transcript page 1526. So how well did the police perform their duties to investigate and report Serb perpetrators of crimes against non-Serbs in 1992? The Chamber admitted into evidence the reports of RS district prosecutor Gacinovic and RS MUP head of the police, Vasic, which analysed the data contained in the criminal case log-books of the municipal and regional police and prosecutors offices from the indictment period. Both witnesses focussed their intention on identifying in these log-books any crimes that fell within the indictment schedules. They also looked for serious crimes committed by Serb perpetrators against non-Serb victims. In particular, they looked at crimes of violence, such as war crimes, murder, rape, serious bodily injury and robberies, as well as grave property crimes such as those comitted with explosive devices. Gacinovic also identified cases of aggravated theft against non-Serbs. Even with this inclusion of this additional crime, her data did not differ significantly from Mr. Vasic's. However, for consistency aggravated thefts had been excluded from the summary I shall now provide. In eight charged municipalities, Pale, Visegrad, Bosanski Samac, Vlasenica, Ilijas, Bileca, Gacko and Kljuc, the police filed no criminal reports for serious crimes committed by Serbs against non-Serbs during the indictment period. Not one. In seven charged municipalities, Vogosca, Bijeljina, Prijedor, Brcko, Donji Vakuf, Kotor Varos, and Skender Vakuf, the police reported just one serious crime committed by Serbs against non-Serbs during the entire indictment period. In Prijedor, Kotor Varos, and Skender Vakuf, the sole crime was an attempted murder, and the attempted murder case in Kotor Varos was reported before the Serbs took over the SJB in the municipality in June of 1992. In two charged municipalities, Zvornik and Doboj, the police reported only two serious crimes committed by Serbs against non-Serbs. And in Sanski Most, the police reported four such crimes. This includes a rape case that Your Honours heard evidence about that resulted in a suspended sentence in 1993 under the reasoning that the victim and the majority of the other Muslims from Sanski Most had moved away, making it less likely that the perpetrator would commit the same or similar crimes in the future. That's P122. In Teslic, the police reported five crimes, serious crimes against non-Serbs. One of the five, the criminal report against the Mice Group did not appear in the police crime log-book for Teslic, but it did appear in the prosecutor's log-book. This is precisely why the crime log-books of both the police and the prosecutor's office were analysed to deliver a complete and accurate picture to the Trial Chamber. Finally, in Banja Luka the log-books reveal that the police filed 18 criminal reports for serious crimes by Serb perpetrators against non-Serb victims during the indictment period. As several of these criminal reports pertain to the same perpetrators for related crimes, the number is, in fact, closer to 14 as we discuss in our final brief. Compared to the other 19 municipalities, 14 criminal cases may seem significant. However, this number pales in comparison to the 4.660 reports filed by the police in Banja Luka in 1992, nor does it adequately account for the large number of non-Serbs who were murdered, robbed and exposed to other acts of violence, often by criminals with direct links to the Serb police and politicians. As described by a number of Banja Luka witnesses as well as the adjudicated facts. For example, the unchallenged adjudicated fact, 1067 states that over 31 non-Serbs were killed by Serb forces in Banja Luka municipality between March and October of 1992. However, the police in Banja Luka reported that for the expanded period of the 1st of January through 20th of December based upon the combined work of the SJB, the CSB and the military police, only three criminal cases were filed against Serb perpetrators for the killing of only eight non-Serbs. This could be found in 1D233. According to this report, five of these eight non-Serb victims were killed by the Sugic brothers and two were killed by Zeljko Ceko. The two murders by Ceko occurred on the 5th of December, 1992, and so are, in addition to those, covered by adjudicated fact 1067. Soon after their initial arrest the Sugic brothers and Ceko were released from detention, allowed to return to the VRS units and were not prosecuted for these murders during the conflict. As evidenced by Ms. Gacinovic's report, the figures I have provided for the 20 charged municipalities did not significantly improve between 1993 and 1995. In other words, it was not just a matter of the police needing time to investigate the crimes comitted against non-Serbs in 1992. Throughout the conflict, these crimes were simply disregarded. Vasic and Gacinovic's data is consistent not only with each other but also with the evidence of former judges, prosecutors and SJB chiefs who testified before this Chamber, as well as echoed in the evidence of the crime-base witnesses. For example, ST-79 testified that the Visegrad police did not interfere in any way with the criminal activities of paramilitaries. And, as a result: "There was no trust whatsoever either in the police or the army. To me, it all seemed that these White Eagles who were doing this throughout the town, and even while the Uzice Corps was there, it appeared to me that they were under their" --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I will slow down. Thank you. And I'll just go back and finish the quote of ST-79: "To me, it all seemed that these White Eagles who were doing this throughout the town, and even while the Uzice Corps was there, it appeared to me that they were under their protection." That's transcript page 2247. This statistical information does not speak by itself. Rather, it is the evidence of the widespread crimes committed against the non-Serb population that gives this data articulation, including the 1.735 non-Serb victims of killing incidents charged in the indictment which represents only a fraction of the total number of non-Serb killings that occurred in the charged municipalities and the many more instances of beatings, rapes, robberies and other violent crimes committed against the non-Serb population. This is the bigger picture, Your Honours in which the police failure to investigate and report crimes must be assessed. What is clear to us from viewing this data 20 years later must have been evident to the accused in 1992 through the daily reports they received and their other sources of information about the work of their subordinates and could only have been terrifyingly obvious to the non-Serb population living amidst these uninvestigated and undeterred crimes. In response to this evidence, the Defence rely on three arguments: First, that the prosecutor's offices and judiciary were not functioning in 1992. Second, that the SJBs lacked the resources to investigate crimes. And, third, that the military had sole jurisdiction to investigate the crimes at issue in this case. None of these arguments is supported by credible evidence. The prosecutor's offices and courts were functioning in 1992. Many without interruption caused by the outbreak of the conflict. For instance, the entries in prosecutor's office log-books for Zvornik, Teslic, Sanski Most, Pale, Bijeljina, and Banja Luka, which also covered Donji Vakuf and Skender Vakuf, showed that these prosecutor's offices were functioning continuously from early April -- early April 1992 onwards. Ms. Gacinovic provided evidence that after the conflict began, she continued to perform her role as deputy prosecutor in Trebinje which had jurisdiction over Bileca until she was appointed Trebinje district prosecutor in August. In Vlasenica, the prosecutor's office log-book shows that the office was open for business from 14 May onwards. With few exceptions, the judicial process was, at most, only briefly disrupted in the municipalities when the Serb authorities fired the non-Serb prosecutors and judges from their positions. Serbs who already held these positions remained in them and the non-Serbs who had left were quickly replaced by other Serbs. For example, at a meeting in May, in Sanski Most, the non-Serb prosecutor and the non-Serb president of the court were dismissed by the Sanski Most SDS leadership and at the same meeting replaced by Serbs. The former non-Serb judge and prosecutor were subsequently arrested and sent to Manjaca camp. The formal appointments of Serb judges and prosecutors by the RS government lagged behind the unofficial appointments at the municipal level. For example, former Visegrad prosecutor, Drasko, began performing the duties of prosecutor at the beginning of September even though his formal appointment did not arrive until October. Nevertheless, the evidence shows that between May and October, the RS government issued appointments to 276 judges and 80 prosecutors. This can be found P1318.23. The Chamber has heard the evidence from a number of prosecutors and judges. And each indicated that not only were their offices functioning despite the difficult conditions but they were willing and able to accept and process any criminal reports filed by the police. Even if the Trial Chamber were to accept the Defence suggestion that the judiciary was slow to begin functioning, one would expect to see a flood of criminal reports filed by -- filed against Serb perpetrators for serious crimes against non-Serbs once these institutions began to function. This did not occur. In fact, the problem was not that the judiciary was dysfunction but rather that the police were simply not filing criminal reports. If we can look at the next slide. As Mandic wrote in his November 1992 report on activities of the RS Ministry of Justice: "We are faced with the fact that a large number of criminal acts have been carried out in Republika Srpska. Official organs have filed a small number of criminal reports to the judicial organs. That is why there is a distinct lack of co-operation between the prosecution organs and the Ministry of Interior." In his report on the crime situation in the area of Teslic municipality from June to September 1992, Teslic prosecutor, Peric, expressed a similar view, writing: "Recorded crime is a fraction of the real crime existing in society today. Most criminal acts remain undiscovered, and many crimes are tolerated by the authorities for various reasons. The prosecutor's office has knowledge of the day-to-day looting of properties, houses and business premises being set on fire and destroyed, armed robbery and murder being committed for base motives, et cetera." He then states: "There is no criminal Prosecution for most of these acts." He further reported: "The destruction of religious buildings is a war crime against civilians because of the way and circumstances in which it was perpetrated. The Serbian people will carry a heavy burden of historical responsibility until the perpetrators of these and similar criminal acts are brought to justice." Peric then demands: "The state and its law enforcement organs must urgently answer the following question: What are the causes of these serious crimes and why are they not being disclosed? An answer to this question should be sought from the command of the Teslic Serbian Brigade and the interior ministry organs." Your Honours, this question was left unanswered until this Tribunal. Mandic and Peric's reports emphasise the essential role of the police in the criminal justice system. Until the police identified the perpetrators of a crime and filed a criminal report against the known perpetrators supported by sufficient evidence, the prosecutors and courts could not initiate criminal proceedings. The prosecutor witnesses who testified during the trial confirmed this was the procedure that existed both prior to and during the conflict. It is also clear from the document evidence. For example, upon receiving the unknown perpetrator criminal report filed by Zupljanin regarding the killing of non-Serb detainees outside Manjaca camp in early August, Deputy Prosecutor Kovacevic sent the report immediately back with the request that the CSB conduct a complete criminal investigation into this case in order to find perpetrators, witnesses, and other individuals, and determine other circumstances related to the commission of this crime. After the perpetrators are found, they must be arrested. As Kovacevic testified, he was merely reminding the police of their independent duty to investigate and report such crimes before he could take any action with regard to the case. As the evidence showed, the police never complied with this request to complete the investigation and, as a result, the police perpetrators in this case were never prosecuted. The police were also aware that it was their duty to identify perpetrators. For example, at the end of Exhibit 1D360, an unknown perpetrator criminal report, CSB Doboj chief, Bjelosevic, informed the prosecutor's office: "Operative action and measures taken so far have not resulted in establishing the identity of the perpetrator or perpetrators. If found, we will send you a separate report." Note that the only document Bjelosevic attached to this report was the court's on-site investigation report. As shown by other examples of unknown perpetrator criminal reports in evidence, the police typically conducted scant, if any, investigation, before filing one of these reports. The filing of a criminal report against an unknown perpetrator, therefore, is -- really served only an administrative purpose, permitting the police log-books to reflect that a criminal report was filed with the prosecutor's office even though the police had not completed their duties to investigate the crime. And, yet, after filing one of these unknown perpetrator reports, the police typically took no further action to solve the case. Ms. Gacinovic testified that her analysis of the unknown perpetrator reports filed with the prosecutor's office for serious crimes against non-Serbs in 1992 showed that, generally, the crimes remained uninvestigated and unsolved by the police throughout the conflict. In the rare instances when the police filed a criminal report against the Serb perpetrator for crimes against non-Serbs, the Defence rightly criticise the prosecutors and courts for failing to indict, try and conflict the perpetrators. The hands of the prosecutors and the courts were by no means clean in this matter. For example, of the 18 criminal reports the police filed in Banja Luka for serious crimes committed by Serbs against non-Serbs, most of the perpetrators were never prosecuted or convicted. The perpetrators charged in at least seven of these reports were released soon after their initial arrest, including Branko Palackovic, Goran Davidovic, Radomir Boskan and the Sugic brothers. As detention in each of these cases was mandatory, the accused had the duty, given their high level positions within the criminal justice system, not to remain idle while these perpetrators were unlawfully released. In fact in one of the cases against Radomir Boskan and two other members of the CSB Banja Luka special police detachment, Zupljanin facilitated the perpetrator's release sending a clear message that the police would not stand in the way of a policy of releasing Serb perpetrators of crimes against non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The accused assert that by failing to act they were just following the rules of procedure regarding detention which gave the judiciary the power to extend detention or release suspects after the initial three-day period. However, their strict adherence to these procedures in the case of Serb perpetrators, such as Palackovic, and the Mice Group contrasted with their attitude toward the indefinite imprisonment of thousands of innocent non-Serbs in police-operated detention facilities throughout the RS. The Defence's second argument, that the police were unable to investigate serious crimes in 1992, is contradicted by the RS MUP's own year-end reports. For example, CSB Banja Luka's year-end report shows that the police in the ARK filed criminal reports for 537 serious criminal offences, using the definition of Gacinovic and Vasic, against 364 perpetrators between April and December 1992. That's found in P624. CSB Sarajevo reported that, for the same period, it filed 118 criminal reports for serious crimes committed by 241 perpetrators. This is found in P740. The RS MUP year-end report indicated that for April through December period, the police filed 494 cases for crimes against life and limb. Incidentally, the RS MUP report also indicates that the police "helped" the military by arresting 9.469 army deserters and persons avoiding military service. This assistance illustrates that the police could arrest fugitives when they put their minds and their resources to it. When these numbers that I have just provided are compared to the findings of Vasic and Gacinovic, that the police filed only 38 criminal reports of serious crimes committed by Serbs against non-Serbs during the indictment period, they place in vivid relief the failure of the police to investigate and report crimes committed against the non-Serb population. Finally, the Defence justify the police failure to investigate and report crimes against the non-Serb population by arguing that these crimes fell within the sole jurisdiction of the military courts. The Stanisic Defence goes so far as making the assertion based on Mandic's testimony that "all persons from 16 to 70 years of age were under the authority of the military judiciary." That can be found in paragraph 591. This notion of absolute military jurisdiction over all crimes flies in the face of the overwhelming evidence in this case. It should be noted that nowhere in their briefs did the Defence address the evidence of former military prosecutor Jovicinac on the military court's jurisdiction. They choose to ignore it completely. As Mr. Jovicinac explained, the primary jurisdiction of the military courts in 1992 was over crimes committed by members of the army. Under Article 3 of the RS Law on the Army, members of the army were limited to soldiers, military cadets, reserve soldiers once they had reported to their military units for duty, and civilian employees under military contract. It did not include ordinary citizens or civilians, did not include police officers, and did it not include reserve soldiers who had not yet joined their military units. The military court's jurisdiction over civilians was limited to the crimes enumerated under Article 13, paragraph 1 of the SFRY Law on The military courts. These crimes related to offenses against the state order, such as armed rebellion, and crimes against the army, such as desertion. The military courts did not have jurisdiction over general crimes committed by civilians against other civilians. In fact, Article 15 of the Law on The military courts states where a soldier and civilian commit a crime as co-perpetrators, the civilian court had jurisdiction over both the military and civilian perpetrators. This is what happened against the Mice Group in Teslic. Article 16 of the Law on Military Courts restricted the jurisdiction of the military courts even further. If a soldier who committed a general crime left the army before an indictment was filed, the civilian courts assumed jurisdiction over that former soldier. The restrictions on the military court's jurisdiction over crimes were practical as well. As the Defence noted, the military courts were not fully functioning until July or August of 1992. And until then, it was incumbent upon the civilian police and courts to investigate all crimes regardless of the status of the perpetrators. Once the military courts began to function their two top priorities were, according to the VRS prosecutor office instructions found in Exhibit 2D107, crimes against the state order and crimes against the army, towards which the military courts and prosecutor's office expended considerable resources as shown by their reports. Their third priority was war crimes. But as we can see from the contemporaneous orders issued by the VRS, such as P1098.20, and P685, as well as illustrated by the cases listed in the VRS prosecutor's annual report for 1992, that is, P1284.55, this priority only pertained to war crimes committed by enemy combatants against Serbs. Your Honours have already heard evidence regarding the work of the VRS military courts in 1992, and admitted into evidence the 1 KK military prosecutor's log-books for this period. This evidence is revealing in three respects. First of all, it shows that the military courts were not exercising jurisdiction over civilians. Secondly, it confirms that the civilian police were not filing criminal reports against Serb perpetrators regardless of their status for serious crimes comitted against non-Serbs with the military prosecutor's office either. And, thirdly, it shows that the military failed to prosecute Serb soldiers for crimes against non-Serbs. They were acting in the same manner as the civilian police. With regard to war crimes, the Law on Military Courts is equally clear. The military exercised jurisdiction only over such crimes committed by soldiers or prisoners of war; that is, enemy combatants. This has been confirmed by witnesses Jovicinac, Drasko and Gacinovic. It is also confirmed by the applicable SFRY regulations on the application of international law of war in armed forces. Paragraph 37 of these regulations assigns military court jurisdiction. It reads: "Trials of military personnel who violate the laws of war which entail criminal liability fall under the jurisdiction of the Yugoslav military courts. If a member of a foreign armed force, that is, an enemy combatant, violates the laws of war he shall be tried by the military court." Noticeably absent from this provision is any indication that the military courts exercise jurisdiction over non-enemy civilian who committed war crimes; that is because they did not. Go to the next slide. That the police had jurisdiction to investigate war crimes committed by civilians is also evidenced by Stanisic's own instructions to his subordinates on 16 May. He wrote: "Measures and activities conducted to document war crimes. These activities must involve collection of information and documents on war crimes against the Serbs. This implies conducting an on-site investigation with the entire team in all cases of crimes against the Serbs, and we particularly point out that a doctor's report must not be forgotten, and photo and video documentation, witness statements, and so on, must be compiled pursuant to the Law on Criminal Procedure." Clearly, Stanisic is instructing his police forces to investigate and file criminal charges for war crimes against Serbs and not just those crimes outside the RS, as the Defence have suggested. The order to conduct an on-site investigation and to comply with the rules of criminal procedure would otherwise make little sense. Your Honours, I'm advised this is probably the best time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to return to the issue of war crimes jurisdiction as this came up many times in the course of this trial. The police jurisdiction over the investigation of war crimes committed by civilians was also established by Stanisic's own witness, Simo Tusevljak, who authenticated a number of criminal reports for war crimes committed against Serbs that he filed with the civilian courts in 1992 and 1993. The Defence contend that it was the policy of the accused that all war crimes should be investigated, regardless of the ethnicity of the victims. As addressed comprehensively in our final brief, the evidence does not support this contention. Rather, following the instructions of the RS MUP leadership, the police focussed their resources exclusively on investigating war crimes committed against Serbs. For example, although Goran Macar claimed that in August 1992 he instructed his RS MUP crime inspectors to investigate all crimes committed by the Yellow Wasps, including war crimes, this was clearly not the case. As Mr. Hannis has discussed, Mr. Macar's testimony is subject to serious questions of credibility. But telling is the list of questions found in the notebook of a RS MUP crime inspector that was used during the interrogations of the Yellow Wasps members. The questions are limited to issues of vehicle thefts, sales of apartments, and lists of unwanted Serbs. None of these questions pertained to war crimes against non-Serbs. This can be found at P403. Equally telling are the Official Notes from the police interviews of the members of the Yellow Wasps, many of which are in evidence in this case, and none of which mention war crimes committed against non-Serbs. If you look at the -- yes, we have the next slide up. Your Honours have already heard evidence that the military prosecutor's office transferred jurisdiction over Dusan Vuckovic, the only Yellow Wasp member who had at one time been in military custody, to the civilian authorities after determining that he was not a member of the VRS. And, yet, the police never fulfilled their duty to supplement their criminal report to include crimes, any crimes, beyond the vehicle thefts which were at issue in the original criminal report they filed with the Bijeljina prosecutor. By the way, this evidence also shows that the military did not exercise jurisdiction, criminal jurisdiction, over paramilitary groups, such as the Yellow Wasps, unless and until these groups were absorbed into the army under Article 9 of the RS Law on the Army. Contrary to the assertions in the Stanisic Defence brief, the police did not hand over the members of the Yellow Wasps to the authorities in Serbia because the prosecutor and the courts in Bijeljina were not functioning. Your Honours have heard from former Bijeljina judge, Simeunovic, who was assigned to this case and nothing in her testimony even suggested that she or the prosecutor were unable to proceed with the prosecution of case against the Yellow Wasps, nor did the police hand over the members of the Yellow Wasps to the Serb authorities. These paramilitaries were released from detention by the investigative judge because, as she explained, the police failed to charge them with anything more serious than vehicle thefts and she was unaware of any war crimes allegations against them. Some of the Yellow Wasps members returned to Zvornik; some left for Serbia; and others were absorbed into the VRS Drina Corps. In its year-end report, the RS MUP confirmed that it -- that its interest in war crimes was limited to those committed against the Serb population. It states: "The focus of the operative work in CSBs and SJBs was on detection, documenting and reporting members of the enemy army who had committed acts of genocide against the Serbian people, torched or destroyed immovable property, cultural and religious monuments and other assets." Turning to police crimes against non-Serb population. Although the RS MUP stated in its year-end report that criminal reports were brought against 29 RS MUP employees between April and December 1992 - this can be found P625, page 27 - Mr. Vasic, utilising the police crime log-books as well as his resources as head of the RS MUP police was able to identify only four cases, four cases, in which police officers were charged with serious crimes against non-Serbs in the indictment municipalities during this period. The first instance was against Radomir Boskan and the two other members of the CSB Banja Luka special police detachment. These are the police officers that Zupljanin played a role in their escape from detention. Contrary to the assertion in the Zupljanin brief, Zupljanin did not request the prosecution of Boskan and his co-perpetrators. The criminal report emanated from the SJB, which, as Your Honours heard, was consistently critical of this special police detachment and the crimes they were committing around the municipality. It did not emanate from the CSB, as it should have, nor were these police officers ever prosecuted for their crimes. The second instance was for a robbery committed by a former member of the CSB Banja Luka special police detachment in October, most likely while he was subordinated to the VRS. The third instance was the criminal report against certain but not all police members of the Mice Group in Teslic. Milan Savic, the CSB Doboj deputy chief who was the police leader of the group, was never charged with these crimes, because the MUP leadership deemed it was not expedient to criminally charge a high-ranking police official. Those officers who were charged were subsequently released from detention and have yet to be prosecuted for the crimes against non-Serbs in Teslic. And the fourth instance was against an SJB Prnjavor police officer for the robbery of a non-Serb. Beyond these four instances, there is no evidence in this case of any other police officers charged with serious crimes against non-Serbs during the indictment period in the 20 indictment municipalities. Equally evident is the accused's failure to discipline their subordinates for crimes against non-Serbs. For example, with regard to CSB Banja Luka, the Chamber heard the evidence of Radomir Rodic regarding the disciplinary cases filed against Serb police officers for offences committed between April and December 1992 that were recorded in a CSB Banja Luka disciplinary case log-book. The Chamber heard that Zupljanin terminated police officers for failing to show up at work, for firing their gun at a stop sign, and killing Serbs. No police officers were disciplined for crimes comitted against non-Serbs. Now, the Zupljanin Defence assert in their brief that Rodic testified that the CSB Banja Luka disciplinary case log-book was incomplete, an incomplete record of the disciplinary reports against police officers. This mischaracterises his evidence. Rodic testified that for some of the entries involving multiple police officers who co-perpetrated the same disciplinary offence, the name of only one of the police officers is listed in the log-book, followed by the notation "and others." Equally incorrect is the Defence's -- Defence assertion that disciplinary proceedings for a criminal offence could not be initiated or completed if a police officer voluntarily resigned. Rodic testified that in such instances disciplinary proceedings continued despite the resignation and there are examples of this is in the CSB Banja Luka disciplinary log-book. With regard to the region covered by CSB Doboj, when Bjelosevic was asked whether he called -- he recalled instituting any disciplinary proceedings against his subordinates for offences related to the mistreatment of non-Serbs, he was only able to recall a case against CSB Doboj crime inspector Solaja. As it turned out, Bjelosevic's disciplinary decision, P2347, showed that he terminated Solaja's employment for the opposite reason: For assisting non-Serbs escape to Belgrade using false identification cards. A disciplinary decision that Stanisic upheld in December. In fact, a protected witness testified that it was not uncommon for Serb police officers to be disciplined for helping non-Serbs during this period. I reference transcript page 3727. In other regions, the Chamber has heard evidence that SJB Vogosca chief Maksimovic was disciplined for TAS vehicle thefts but not for the crimes that occurred under his watch at the bunker and other locations, other detention facilities in Vogosca. And SJB Visegrad police officer Sredoje Lukic was disciplined for releasing a Serb prisoner and not reporting to work on occasions, but not for the house fire on Pionirska Street or any of the other crimes that he and police officer Milan Lukic committed against the non-Serb population in Visegrad. The Stanisic Defence contend that Stanisic lacked the authority to initiate or decide in the first instance disciplinary proceedings against his subordinates. This was not the case. As Tomislav Kovac testified, Stanisic "was the one person who had to make the decisions on both accepting people into the service and dismissing them from the service." Transcript page 27076. When Judge Hall asked Dragan Andan whether it was possible for the minister to both initiate and decide a disciplinary case, Andan answered in the affirmative. Transcript page 21780. In fact, Article 115 of the RS Law on Internal Affairs gave the minister the power to decide who could initiate disciplinary proceedings. And Article 5 of the RS MUP war time disciplinary procedures stated that a disciplinary case "may be initiated at the initiative of any worker of an internal affairs organ," which must have included the minister himself as well. 1D54. Furthermore, there are examples where Stanisic did exercise his authority to discipline his subordinates. As Mr. Hannis pointed out, he dismissed SJB Bijeljina chief Andan for failing to follow proper procedures regarding the use of a confiscated poker machine and he dismissed SJB Bijeljina crime police chief Danilo Vukovic for drunk and disorderly behaviour at a bar. Your Honours, although the ultimate punishment under the police disciplinary procedures termination of employment was an insufficient form of punishment for any of the police crimes alleged in the indictment, the failure of the accused to ensure that their subordinates were disciplined for crimes against non-Serbs is relevant for at least three reasons: First, had they disciplined their subordinates for these crimes, it would have sent a message to the police force that such crimes would not be tolerated. Secondly, it would have shown to the non-Serb population that the RS MUP was serious about ensuring that the police protect all citizens indiscriminately. And, thirdly, the accused failure to discipline their subordinates for these crimes reflected their more general disregard for crimes committed against the non-Serb population. I want to briefly address the Defence suggestion that Stanisic's orders beginning sometime after the 11th July collegium meeting to replace RS MUP personnel -- or, to place RS MUP personnel at the disposal of the army was a form of disciplinary punishment. First, these orders were primarily directed at augmenting the army with those police officers who had outlived their usefulness to the RS MUP, as Stanisic and General Mladic had agreed during the July meeting that Mr. Hannis discussed. This can be seen by his -- Stanisic's 27 July order - that's 1D176 - in which Stanisic classified both criminal and unneeded police officers as surplus persons to be sent to the army. In addition, if Stanisic was serious about preventing or punishing police crimes, his orders would have expressly and explicitly stated that these surplus officers must be arrested, subjected to both disciplinary and criminal proceedings. They do not, nor did Stanisic instruct the police to inform the VRS of the criminal conduct of police officers they were putting at the army's disposal. Thus, a police officer who mistreated non-Serbs at Omarska or at Luka camp could have very well ended up guarding non-Serb detainees at Manjaca or Batkovic. All Stanisic was doing was shifting a problem from one organ to another. In order to justify their inaction in punishing their subordinates, both accused argue that the police committed these crimes while resubordinated to the military. Ms. Korner has already addressed how the evidence does not support the Defence suggestion that the police were almost entirely resubordinated to the military during the indictment period. But even if the Trial Chamber were to accept the Defence's extreme interpretation of resubordination, this did not diminish the accused's authority or duty to prevent and punish their police subordinates. The Defence are misguided in their assumption that the principle of unity of command means that a resubordinated police officer cannot have two superiors. As a matter of law, a subordinate can be under the command of more than one superior, and each superior can be held responsible for the subordinate's crimes. I direct the Trial Chamber's attention to the Strugar Trial Chamber Judgement paragraph 367. Moreover, there is nothing novel about RS MUP commanders retaining control over MUP force, even when such forces have been temporarily resubordinated into the army. In the Popovic case, the Trial Chamber found that the RS MUP forces resubordinated to the VRS still retained their internal chain of command, and as a result held Ljubomir Borovcanin, deputy commander of the RS MUP special police brigade, had effective control over such resubordinated MUP units. I direct the Trial Chamber's attention to paragraphs 3, 184, 1567 to 1569. Your Honours, while this is not controlling authority, the Prosecution submits it is highly persuasive. Now, while the VRS may have assumed responsibility for assigning combat tasks to resubordinated police officers during a particular combat operation, the RS MUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Olmsted. I see that you have cited Strugar and Popovic which you admit may be persuasive to us in our findings, but your own proposition that, as a matter of law, a subordinate can be under the command of more than one superior, and each superior can be held responsible for the subordinate's crimes, is there anything in the -- either the evidence or the representations before this Tribunal to which you could refer us to support your assertion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I mean, Your Honours, the position of the Prosecution is that the police maintained really singleness of command over the MUP forces except for the purposes of operations on the front lines. An so -- the evidence -- we shall -- we suggest the evidence reflects that. What I'm simply proposing is that there is jurisprudence before this Tribunal that it makes no difference because you can have parallel chains of commands and there is quite a bit of jurisprudence on that issue. To go into more detail, we would ask that we be given a few minutes, perhaps tomorrow, to address this and point the Trial Chamber to the places where we deal with it in our final brief as well as in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Olmsted, but I was going to ask Your Honours at the end of today, in the light of what Mr. Zecevic raised dated in respect to Mr. Hannis's address on the Stanisic interview that Your Honour -- even though Your Honours have ruled that we can't do this in writing, Your Honours, we would say that, of course, we filed our briefs at the same time. We didn't know what the Defence were going to say about the law. In the light of the this and the intervention to Mr. Hannis's address, we would ask that on Friday, Your Honours grant some time to deal with matters of law. Can I just put it that way at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It may be appear that that may be a sensible course to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The RS MUP retained ultimate command over their police officers and this is shown by the evidence of -- that both Stanisic and Zupljanin had the power to organise their subordinates into war units and provide them with training and equipment, the power to decide whether and when to resubordinate police units to the VRS, the power to participate in the command of combat operations of these war units, as Zupljanin did in Orasje in November of 1992, and the power to withdrew the units from the front lines when they deemed it necessary as Ms. Korner discussed during her statement. Indeed Stanisic's 15 May order establishing war units instructed that all such units be under the direct command of an RS MUP commander, and he also created a staff headed by himself to oversee these units. These measures were clearly taken to maintain RS MUP control over any police units engaging in combat activities with the VRS. The accused also retained the authority to discipline and criminally charge police officers for crimes committed while resubordinated. With regard to disciplinary measures, as the ultimate punishment was termination, this punishment logically could only have been meted out by the RS MUP. Even in 1994, when the RS law was amended to place the RS MUP within the armed forces during a war or imminent threat of war, the law explicitly preserved for the RS MUP the power to discipline its police officers. That's L317. With regard to criminal investigations, as Mr. Jovicinac explained, the resubordinated police officer did not fall within the definition of military personnel under the Law of the army. And, therefore, they were not subject to military court jurisdiction for general crimes or for that matter, war crimes. This made sense. A police officer was typically resubordinated for only a short period of time, one, two, maybe three weeks. And under Article 16 of the SFRY Law on the Military Courts it would have been unlikely that an indictment could be filed against him before he returned to his regular police duties. Moreover, as Mr. Jovicinac suggested, the prosecution of police crimes was a delicate issue as RS MUP had a separate chain of command. The VRS was extremely hesitant to assume jurisdiction over police crimes, leaving it to the police hierarchy to address them. This is precisely why General Talic sent a request to CSB Banja Luka to take action against police deserters in October of 1992. That's 1D411. If we can look at -- yes, we have the slide on the screen. In fact, this Chamber has in evidence an example of Zupljanin exercising disciplinary and criminal jurisdiction over police officers for crimes committed while resubordinated. In a 18 October dispatch regarding police who on 17 October refused to obey VRS orders while resubordinated, Zupljanin ordered that: "All workers who refused to obey orders were to be suspended and criminal measures filed against them." If we can look at the next slide. To show that these were not just hollow words, if we look at the CSB Banja Luka disciplinary case log-book, we see an entry against Ljubisa Nikolic and others from SJB Gradiska for a violation committed on 17 October, 1992, and the result was termination of employment. Finally, I want to address the Defence contention that certain of the more notorious SJB chiefs, such as Todorovic, Drljaca and Koroman were untouchable, immune to any attempts by the accused to discipline, remove or criminally investigate them. The Defence rely primarily on two arguments: First, they contend that because the Crisis Staffs appointed these individuals SJB chief, the accused were powerless to discipline them. Mr. Hannis addressed this issue. He discussed Variant A and B instructions. And, in fact, they called for in the interim period when a municipality was taken over for the municipal authorities to appoint SJB chiefs temporarily until the RS MUP was in a position to take over the duty of appointing police in those particular municipalities, not all of them but some of them. Stanisic was aware of this, and that is why on 25 April he issued a decision in which he ordered CSB chiefs to obtain preceding agreement of the Ministry of Interior before distribution of employees onto next jobs and assignments. Your Honour, the operative word being "next." To avoid ambiguity, he clarified under item 4: "The decisions which deal with taking over the distribution of the employees within the MUP (Ministry of Interior) of the Serbian Republic BH and were issued before issuing this decision have all legal effects on persons named." In other words, Stanisic was ratifying the prior appointments of SJB chiefs and other members of the police leadership. If, as the Stanisic Defence assert, Todorovic was appointed by the Bosanski Samac Crisis Staff on 28 March and if Koroman was appointed before 1 April by the BiH MUP, then Stanisic's 25 April order effectively confirmed those appointments. With regard to Drljaca, the accused ratified his appointment on 30 July 1992, applying it retroactively to 29 April; that is, the day before the take-over, the Serb take-over, of Prijedor. Contrary to the assertion by the Stanisic Defence, Zupljanin's mention in the written decision that this appointment was made with prior approval of Stanisic was not just standard language. We can see this by comparing Drljaca's appointment with that of Dusan Jankovic as commander of SJB Prijedor. Under Stanisic's 25 April order, both positions, both appointments required the formal approval of the RS MUP but we can see that while Drljaca's appointment mentions the prior approval of the minister, Jankovic appointment does not. Your Honours, there are examples in evidence where the RS MUP removed SJB chiefs who were initially appointed by the municipal authorities. Mr. Hannis has already mentioned Marinko Vasilic who -- there is no contention that he was appointed by the Zvornik Crisis Staff. However Stanisic had no problem removing him in October or November 1992 for failing to report to the RS MUP. And while the Prosecution maintains that Boro Maksimovic, chief of SJB Vogosca, was ap pointed by Stanisic, the Defence contend that the Crisis Staff appointed him. If this is the case, this is yet another example where the RS MUP was able to remove a SJB chief appointed by municipal authorities. The second argument raised by the Defence is that it would have been dangerous for the accused to remove these SJB chiefs from their positions in 1992 through the use of force or other means. This raises a question, Your Honours: Dangerous to whom? If the Defence are suggesting it would have been dangerous to the accused or their police subordinates, the RS Law on Internal Affairs required them to put the safety of citizens before their own. And, indeed, the police did not hesitate putting their lives on the line when it came to the issue of vehicle thefts. If the Defence are suggesting that the safety of the civilian population would have been placed at risk, then they are ignoring the evidence that the lives of the non-Serb population were already in grave danger and remained so, so long as these SJB chiefs remained in their positions. While it is easy to -- while it is easy to pass the blame to these SJB chiefs, particularly in the case of Todorovic and Drljaca --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speaker please slow down for the sake of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- who are no longer alive to provide evidence to the contrary, the fact is that these SJB chiefs were kept in their positions because they were effective and essential participants in the joint criminal enterprise. Recall that Zupljanin was part of the ARK delegation that visited Omarska and other detention facilities in Prijedor in July. Immediately after that visit, Brdjanin announced to the media on behalf of the delegation, that Prijedor is an example of a job well done. P1378. In an interview before assuming his new position as RS MUP Assistant Minister in 1993 Drljaca showed no signs that he placed himself above his superiors or the Law on Internal Affairs. He stated: "If something has not been done well, then I am to be replaced, not them," referring to his subordinates "because they were carrying out my orders, and the orders of Banja Luka CSB ... and the MUP minister." Contrary to the assertion by the Zupljanin Defence, Drljaca was not removed by the Prijedor Crisis Staff; rather, Drljaca stated during his interview that he urged the RS MUP minister to replace him in order to allow the dust to settle. Stanisic's actions and inaction during his second term as RS MUP minister in 1994 reflect his state of mind in 1992 with regard to these SJB chiefs. He appointed Drljaca chief of CJB Prijedor in April 1994. He appointed Koroman chief of CSB Sarajevo police tasks and duties in January 1994 and chief inspector of RS MUP police special operations in May 1994, and as for Todorovic, he remained in his position as SJB Bosanski Samac chief throughout Stanisic's second term as minister. Your Honours it is not that the accused were unsuccessful in their efforts to remove the SJB chiefs from their positions or to punish them for their crimes. It is that they took no actions to do so, but, instead, chose to praise and promote them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order that the general public doesn't think that the Office of the Prosecutor is entirely staffed by white male North Americans, I'm going to conclude what the Office of the Prosecutor wants to say in this case. And, Your Honours, I want to do so, please, by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I would remind you that you have 37 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I am well aware of that, Your Honour. We have been timing ourselves very careful and checking with the Court. Your Honours, we want to look, in conclusion, in a little deal at one of the major and most notorious massacres that took part in this -- in 1992 and which is one of the crimes charged in this indictment, and that is that of Koricanske Stijene. Your Honour, because, really, what happened there on the 21st of August, 1992, and thereafter encapsulates all the themes we say that we have attempted to address throughout the course of the last day and a half: The unwarranted attacks on non-Serb areas; the rounding of unarmed civilians by a mixture of police and military personnel; their incarceration in a detention facility; the loading onto buses of prisoners to take them out of Serb-controlled, Serb-held areas; the whole-scale killing of those being transported; and the subsequent, deliberate, flagrant omission by both of the accused in this case to do anything about the known killers or discipline the officer who was direct in charge of them. Your Honours, very few people, very few men, survived the killing. One of them was ST-65 from whom Your Honours heard, if only briefly, but his testimony in a previous case came in. He was a native of the Prijedor municipality, who, on the 20th of July, was taken with his father from his village by armed uniformed men, some of whom were in the olive-drab-type camouflage uniforms and some in police. He was able to identify a photograph of the police uniforms and he had reason to know from his background, which, as he is a protected witness, I'm not going to go into, what police uniforms looked like. He and the rest of his village in response to the disarmament order had given up all of their weapons and uniforms some time before he was taken. And he and his father and the other men, not only from his village but from elsewhere, this was part of the attack on the Brdo area of Prijedor, was taken to Trnopolje. One month later, buses arrived and the prisoners were told to board them. They were driven from Trnopolje to the cross roads where Banja Luka and Kozarac, where, effectively, the roads there meet, and there they linked up with other buses. The convoy then set off towards Travnik. The escort, and there is no dispute about this at all, Your Honours, was the Prijedor or part of the Prijedor Intervention Platoon. Whilst they were on the buses, the prisoners were robbed of their valuables and money that they had left. Yet another facet of the persecutory activities of the RS MUP during this period. Once they reached the area of Koricanske Stijene, the men were ordered out of the bus, and in military fashion, two by two, were ordered towards the edge of the abyss and ordered to kneel down there. Can we have a look for a moment - I know Your Honours have been there - just to remind yourself of the view that these men must have had as they looked down on the road over the abyss. The marking, of course, were made by one of the witnesses. This is how ST-65 described what had happened to him, not in this trial, but in the previous trial, and the transcript is P1769-01 at page 6905: "When we knelt down, we could see this enormous abyss below us and then I could hear the person saying, person behind me, one of the Intervention Platoon, 'Here we exchange dead for the dead and living for the living' ... that's when the shooting started from fire-arms. I saw that people were starting falling down into the abyss and then my father pushed me there in the precipice." He fell, became unconscious and found himself, when he woke from the -- when he regained consciousness, with a broken ankle. Shortly thereafter, whilst he was still there, men came down, he said, and were shooting survivors in the head. He does not know why or how he survived. Eventually he managed to crawl to an inhabited area. He was found there by member of the military. He was taken to Skender Vakuf and from there to Banja Luka hospital. On the way, a statement was taken from him, and he said tape-recorded. He was able to recognise some of the Intervention Platoon who were involved in the massacre, a massacre of approximately 200 men, including the witness's father. Whilst he was in hospital, in Banja Luka, he gave a further statement, as did two or three of the other survivors. So, we have, in hospital, witnesses, victims in Banja Luka. What happened about the investigation? The killings were reported in the evening of the same day, the 21st of August, to Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic when he came back from a meeting at headquarters. He was the officer in charge of the unit that was stationed in the area. He immediately went out, although it was night, inspected the area, saw the blood, and he sent a telegram, both to the 1st Krajina Corps and to the CSB Banja Luka. And this is the telegram that he sent addressed to the 1st Krajina Corps. He talks about the refugee convoy moving towards Travnik: "The Prijedor and Sanski Most CSB police were escorting the convoy." So clearly he had received by the evening of that date, very, very accurate information: "At the same time, the convoy stopped in the area of Koricanske Stijene, refugees were taken out and genocide against the civilians was committed by killing them in various ways and throwing them into the river canyon." "Numbers of police members participated in the liquidation. The units an individuals from the 22nd Light Infantry Brigade had nothing to do with this." "And we ask the following measures be taken." One of the features that we've been attempting to explain through this case is that the shovelling of blame elsewhere, and here the army saying, Absolutely nothing to do with us. Correctly as it turned out on this occasion. This is police. Zupljanin was aware of what had happened by the very next day. The Defence quote -- forgive me, Your Honour, what he said to Mr. Buhavac, apparently with approbation. And this is paragraph 65. Mr. Buhovac was the man who died, the technician, forensic technician, from Banja Luka and his statement, however OTP objections, was admitted -- his interview, rather, with the OTP. Paragraph 65, the Defence say this of the Zupljanin final brief: "Zupljanin was also notable for his efforts in investigating crimes comitted by Serbs against non-Serbs. When he heard about the massacre at Koricanske Stijene, his first reaction, as recorded by Branko Buhovac in an interview by the Office of the Prosecutor, was one of 'horror' with him explaining to Buhovac, chief of forensics in Banja Luka," forgive the expression, but I think it has to be repeated, "fuck. Some jerks did something stupid." Now Your Honours may think that is a thoroughly inappropriate remark to have been made under any circumstances when you're being told that your police have massacred 200 people. It is, however, possibly explicable by the fact that this happened roughly two weeks after the camps at Prijedor had been exposed to international attention by ITN and other news media, and, therefore, no doubt, the Bosnian Serbs were very concerned about the possibility that this might attract even more unfavorable publicity. According to the witnesses who attended subsequent meetings, it was openly admitted the words used by at least one witness was "boasted" by Drljaca that it was Prijedor police who had committed the killings. The only orders given by Zupljanin at this stage were that the bodies should be recovered, and we would suggest that he had at the back of his mind, as I say, the international media. Clearly as the scale of the massacre became clear, higher level government officials began to attend meetings at Banja Luka. Deputy Minister Avlijas was at one, Defence Minister Subotic at another. Again, the focus was not on the arrests of the perpetrators but on the recovery of the bodies. On the 31st of August, Mico Stanisic who had been told, according to what he said in interview to the Office of the Prosecutor, some three days after what had happened issued his one and only order in respect of this killing. It is P870. No attempts to pursue the matter or give instructions to Assistant Minister Kovac or Macar after this order were made. Zupljanin then waited until the 11th of September to sent this order to Drljaca, and this is P1380 and it combines the two. Mr. Stanisic's order issued on the 31st of August, you can see, orders a full investigation in accordance with the laws and regulations of the killing of 150 Muslim people in the area of Skender Vakuf: "You will inform this ministry immediately about the results of the investigation, and in the case that the above-mentioned allegation is confirmed, you will start legal proceedings against the perpetrators." Well, by that stage, everybody knew and had been discussing that it was the Prijedor Intervention Platoon who had committed these murders. No explanation is given or was available to us as to why that order wasn't forwarded until the 11th of September. Between the 11th of September and the 13th of October, Zupljanin and Drljaca engaged in a correspondence over the names and whereabouts of the officers who were involved. And those are set out at correspondence set out in paragraph 990 of our final brief. On the 8th of September, Zupljanin sent an unknown perpetrator report to the Banja Luka prosecutor. That's P1567. The report makes absolutely no mention of the fact that Prijedor police were involved, although that was known to all, and, in particular, Zupljanin by the 8th of September. On the 30th of September, the prosecutor's office asked the police to continue investigating and to identify and arrest suspects. That was it. Nothing further was done; neither by Mico Stanisic, to make any further inquiries, nor by Zupljanin. The matter didn't resuscitate itself, really, until 1999 when the file was reopened. When Mico Stanisic returned as minister in 1994, he took no action about it. His reaction to all of this, when interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor, was to blame Zupljanin. The -- two accused in this case have not run a -- sometimes known in -- in the common law world as a cut-throat Defence, in other words, where each blames the other, they have run a Defence together. However, in -- when he was first interviewed, Mico Stanisic had this to say. The first reference to it is in P -- no, it's not up. P2302, at pages 2 to 3, when he was being interviewed and asked questions, he said this -- the context, I suppose, we ought to put in is: When he returned in 1994 he had given -- been given information about war crimes and he was being asked what information that he had, and he started off by saying, this at is page 1, that he: "... personally did not have any information about war crimes. There were public rumours, particularly through the media, and particularly because I was in a position here to listen to what foreign and local reporters were saying." At page 2, he went on himself to bring up Koricanske Stijene: "In 1992, when Koricanske Stijene happened, I did whatever I could in my capacity. I sent an order to inform both the military and civil because I didn't know whether it was the jurisdiction of the civilian or military office of the prosecutor, an order that an on-site investigation should be carried out and that all measures envisaged by law should be undertaken to resolve this case, to solve this case," and we've seen the one and only order. He goes onto give a long answer and then said this: "Certain activities" -- and this is at page 3: "Certain activities were conducted amongst the investigating judge and the prosecutor between 1990 and late 1992, at the end of 1992. But in 1993, all activities related to this case were terminated. That was one of the fundamental reasons why I removed Stojan Zupljanin from his position." He was asked: Why you removed him from his position in 1994, which we say is incorrect, in any event, "because I had left in 1992 so it wasn't possible for me." And then he goes onto deal with that. Later, and this is at P2310, at pages 20 to 22, he said: "It was of special interest for me to solve Koricanske Stijene, which was what I mentioned two or three days ago. And for that reason, I assigned all chiefs of centres at that time to different tasks, because I was not able to exclude them." He is asked what he meant by "exclude," and he said: "I didn't have such authority, but I moved all the chiefs of CSBs where they worked so they wouldn't represent an obstacle to the investigation." And one of the themes that has come out on this case is that nobody who knowingly committed crimes ever seems to have been removed. They all got promoted; Drljaca being the obvious example. "As soon as I had replaced Stojan Zupljanin from the position of chief of centre, he went to Krajina in Croatia to become the advisor to Martic." And then he went onto deal with -- he was then asked: "Q. Were there any particular chiefs that you were concerned about? "A. Stojan Zupljanin. But a commission was set up. Actually, the chiefs of administration were ordered together with their teams and inspectors to analyse the work of the MUP from the beginning until 1994. "Q. I'm sorry. You were concerned, in particular, about Zupljanin and no other CSB heads? "A. Well, all -- through Zupljanin, the idea was to be a obtain the information through Zupljanin why nothing was done in 1993 regarding the case of Koricanske Stijene, because both then and now, I am convinced there was an influence. Someone did influence the hiding of the perpetrators or trying to cover for the perpetrators." Now, Your Honours, we do not ask Your Honours to rely on that at all. Indeed, Mr. Zupljanin wasn't present at that interview to confirm or deny it. We say it's yet another example of trying to shift the blame, his own responsibility, to someone else. In September and October -- or, I'm sorry, in September or October - I think it's October but it's not clear - Zupljanin was interviewed, as was Talic, about this incident, not surprisingly once the internationals got to hear of it, despite all attempts to stop them, they pounced on it. Was interviewed by a reporter from "ABC Night-Line" at P1359. We can start with Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Reporter: ... General Momir Talic. "Our investigation showed that no soldiers participated. "Reporter: Having cleared themselves, General Talic's men turned over both survivors to the police in Banja Luka. But police chief Stojan Zupljanin told me: "We have no living witnesses who can confirm or deny the incident. "Reporter: At least Zupljanin admits the incident occurred. He says it's under investigation and he showed us files of evidence, even let us watch his ballistics expert examine bullets that were found at the scene. He promises: "The Serbian people will see to it that all the guilty parties are tried in a court of ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it has been slightly chopped off, but ... Your Honours, that was lie after lie. There are no living witnesses to Zupljanin's certain knowledge, sitting in the hospital -- the witness who we've spoken about was in hospital for some months and eventually, because he was so negligently treated - putting it at its lowest - he lost his foot, and the investigation, they don't know who it is. They knew perfectly well who had done it. The Intervention Platoon police who had committed the killings were sent out of the way to Han Pijesak. However, within weeks they were returning to Prijedor to work, to the SJB. The leader of that platoon who gave the orders, a man named Miroslav Paras, was actually given an award by Karadzic for his police work in 1992. And Drljaca, the man in charge of the SJB who boasted about the killings, as Your Honours have heard, was promoted and also given a medal in the course of some of these awards. Your Honours, in the light of what we have just gone through, we suggestion that the Defence assertion that Zupljanin was notable for his efforts in investigating crimes committed by Serbs against non-Serbs, with specific reference to this crime, doesn't even begin to get off the ground. In conclusion, Your Honour, the Stanisic Defence, at paragraph 20, invited you to conclude that the Mico Stanisic of 20 years ago is the same person that the Trial Chamber has been observing during the Trial. That's the word used. We suggest that's not a helpful observation. Because, in effect, it's inviting you to say that because there are no outbursts from the dock, or anything like that, if is, as is said earlier in that paragraph, you are to conclude he was not capable of committing the crimes for which he is charged. Apart from how that is supposed to reflect on his co-accused, we suggest, is obviously not the proper way of looking at the matter. Along the same lines, the final brief for Stojan Zupljanin prays in aid his consistent and sincere expressions of sympathy for those who suffered, adding: "It is notable that such behaviour is not a regular practice before this Tribunal." Leaving aside that this Trial Chamber has no idea what is regular practice in other courts or what's happened in other trials, nor, indeed, have any way of gauging how sincere those expressions were, again, we say it is not a proper way of asking the Trial Chamber to deal with the case. We submit that you have to look at the evidence of what the accused did and said during and after the relevant period. An objective look at that evidence, we submit, will show that the two accused were fully committed to and did everything in their power to carry out the objectives of the joint criminal enterprise, in the full knowledge that it would involve the commission of the crimes alleged. Your Honour, the joint criminal enterprise could not have been put into effect without their commitment, their personal commitment, and the commitment of the forces that were under their command. I can do no better than repeat the words of Mr. Olmsted: "During periods of ethnic conflict, the police role in protecting citizens, particularly those persecuted, is vital." In this case, we say, on the evidence that Your Honours have heard, they did the very opposite of what their duty should have been, and they joined in the persecution, the killings, and the like. Not, of course, in their personal capacity; but, if anything, their role was more important, because they were the ones who gave the orders and set the standards. And it's for those reasons that we say, and have said in our brief, that the proper sentence that they should receive, each of them, is one of life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Zecevic, can you usefully make use of the 15 minutes - well, 13 minutes - remaining today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have a few technical issues which I can deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Your Honours, in our closing arguments, we will be addressing the final brief of the Prosecution, their closing arguments, and we'll give an overview of our final brief and our positions in respect of Mr. Stanisic's criminal responsibility. Before I begin, I have several information [as interpreted] to share of technical nature. For the sake of the transcript, let me say that we identified an error in our final brief at page 247, paragraph 683, under Roman V, where, instead of number 675, number 677 should read. Yesterday at page 6 of the transcript, Ms. Korner referred to paragraph 53 of our final brief, specifically the first sentence of the paragraph which lacks a reference. In fact, it is true that the reference contained in footnote 90 does not relate to the statement in the paragraph. Ms. Korner is right, and we are grateful to her for drawing our attention to it. It's a technical error. In fact, the reference to this statement was testimony by Witness Mandic at T -- transcript page 9626 to 9634, and it was listed in the next footnote, footnote 91, which accompanies paragraph number 54. I do apologise for these errors, which were the result of the fact that we had to shorten our submissions to meet the word limit. Likewise, at page 7 of yesterday's transcript, Ms. Korner referred to paragraph 99 of our brief, which, according to her, related to 1D116. It was stated that the conclusion made in that sentence did not follow from the document referenced. However, the reference which underlies the conclusion is the comment made by Witness Vlaski in relation to 1D116, and the correct reference for that is contained in footnote 161. Your Honours, before I proceed with our closing arguments, I would like to present to the Trial Chamber our position with respect to what Mr. Hannis had to say at page 20 of today's transcript. However, in view of what the guidance has been by the Trial Chamber in response to Ms. Korner's question a moment ago, should I perhaps leave it for a later time? For Friday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we haven't fully decided how we're going to deal with that. So if it's convenient, you can deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours. Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Your Honours, in presenting arguments, at page 20, Mr. Hannis made a comment about the inferences that the Trial Chamber should draw or the elements that it should take into consideration, in view of the fact that the accused in this case did not testify. I rose to object, and I apologise for that again. I'm not in the habit of interrupting anyone's closing submissions, but I felt that I needed to do so. At any rate, I will present our submissions on this issue briefly. In the course of this trial, I was able to identify three references for our position and Article 21, para (4)(g) -- or Rule 21, para (4)(g) of our Statute. I also have some of the ICTY jurisprudence that I will list here and comment on briefly. In view of the fact that they are in English, I will read them out in the original. [In English] Perisic Trial Judgement: "Under specific evidentiary consideration, (A), statements of the accused ..." it's paragraph 35: Article 21(4)(g) of the Statute provides that an accused shall not be compelled to testimony against himself. In the present case, the accused elected not to give evidence during the trial. In accordance with the existing jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber, in the determination of his guilt or innocence, has not drawn any inference from his silence." The Trial Chamber here, in footnote 51, cites the relevant -- the relevant jurisprudence. Second is Popovic Trial Judgement, against under specific evidentiary considerations, paragraph 17: "Article 21(4)(g) of the Statute provides that an accused shall not be compelled to testify. No adverse inferences were drawn against the accused who exercised their right to remain silent." And, finally, Milutinovic Trial Judgement, paragraph 41: "Evidence of accused. Of the six co-accused, only Lazarevic elected to give evidence during the trial. In accordance with Article 21 (4)(g) of the Statute the Chamber has drawn no adverse findings from the other accused's decision not to give evidence." [Interpretation] Your Honour, our position is that it is absolutely unacceptable to - before this Tribunal, in view of the provisions of the Statute and clear jurisprudence - discuss this issue at all, since various Trial Chambers and the Appeals Chamber discussed the ICTY law -- case law plentifully and in view of the rights guaranteed by the Statute for the accused appearing before the Tribunal. Your Honours, I would like to move onto our closing arguments, and with your leave, I should like to do so tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: On this point that you have just made, Mr. Zecevic, the question I'm asked -- you maybe thought to be unfair in the sense that I didn't challenge Mr. Hannis with the reservation that I'm now about to articulate when he made his proposition. But what I understood him to be saying was not that he was inviting the Chamber to draw adverse inferences against the accused in their failure to give evidence; and, as you say, there is adequate jurisprudence in support of that. But he was inviting a contrast between the fact of this choice and the representations which the accused would have given in their -- in their interviews at an earlier stage in these proceedings by the OTP. And I confess that the reason why I didn't ask Mr. Hannis about that is because I'm not clear myself as to what the evidential value of those earlier interviews is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I will try to explain as much as I can. The point of the matter, Your Honour, is the fact that Mico Stanisic voluntarily give the interview to the Office of the Prosecutor. Over five days. He gave his interview -- he was asked whether this interview can be used in -- in a trial against you, he says, I agree, you can use all this in a trial against me. The Office of the Prosecutor, by the bar table motion, offers, offers the interview of the accused Stanisic given on that particular occasion for the -- for the truth of its contents. It offers it to the -- to the Trial Chamber. That is what -- what the bar table -- bar table motion says. Therefore, in our opinion, this is the Prosecutor's evidence which they offered. We accepted it because it is our client, and we have nothing to be afraid of. In fact, we submit that we stand by his interview, and we stand by his interview throughout our Defence -- our Defence presentations and throughout this whole trial. Now, Mr. Hannis's -- my understanding was that Mr. Hannis is trying again to -- to challenge whether the -- whether -- whether you should -- whether you should give weight or trust the contents of that interview. But, again, Your Honours, it's -- it's -- it's our position that the interview has been explicitly offered by the Office of the Prosecutor. It is not the Defence who offered this interview. Perhaps in that situation, he might have the grounds to -- to make such an argument. But in case where the Office of the Prosecutor, by bar table motion, asks that this document be admitted in their case as their proof, I don't see how he can make this argument now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask, then are Your Honours going -- because we do have a reply on all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was going to say that it looks suspiciously as if we're going -- that this is going to be on the agenda for Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But we will see. So we take the adjournment, to reconvene in this courtroom at 10.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
